utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: So good morning to everybody. We resume the hearing in -- that was adjourned yesterday in the case Prosecutor versus Hadzihasanovic and Kubura. We heard yesterday the appeal from Kubura and the appeal from the Prosecution. We will hear today the appeal from Hadzihasanovic and we'll give the floor to counsel for Hadzihasanovic for their submissions. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Judges. Allow me to begin by withdrawing our urgent motion, which was filed on 3 December on the basis of information which was received from the Chamber's legal officer. This was a motion dealing with last-minute translations. My submissions this morning concerning the appeal of General Hadzihasanovic will be presented as follows: Firstly, the third ground of appeal, related to counts 3 and 4 for events in Bugojno; secondly, the fifth ground of appeal, related to grounds 3 and 4 for events in Orasac. I will then address specific issues in the fourth ground of appeal very briefly, concerning events which -- for count 4, in music school. As for grounds 1 and 2, which refer to the fairness of the trial, we stand by our written pleadings. If the Judges have any questions concerning these two grounds, I will be glad to answer. Time permitting, Mr. President, I will address one further issue at the end; and namely, the Trial Chamber's adjudication on the appellant's Rule 98 bis motion at the end of the Prosecution case. Before moving on to my first topic, there are three preliminary remarks which we submit have a bearing on the adjudication of this appeal. Firstly, it is our submission that the multiple measures taken by General Hadzihasanovic to prevent his subordinates from committing crimes or to punish them, as they appear on the record, must be taken into consideration when assessing the findings of the Trial Chamber as part of this appeal. Secondly, it is our submission that in this case the Prosecution had the burden to prove beyond a reasonable doubt the failure to take necessary and reasonable measures and that at no time it was for the appellant to show that measures were indeed taken. Thirdly, we take the view that fair trial issues raised as part of our second ground of appeal did have a bearing and should be considered in assessing the Trial Chamber's findings in this appeal. I move to the third ground of appeal, related to counts 3 and 4 for the events in Bugojno. My submissions on this ground will comprise four parts: First, the question posed by the Appeals Chamber in the Scheduling Order; second, the errors committed by the Trial Chamber which we submit they -- the Trial Chamber committed, concerning the measures as they were taken in Bugojno by 307 Brigade and the municipal public prosecutor in response to criminal acts committed by soldiers of the 307 Brigade. The third part will address the alleged errors committed by the Trial Chamber concerning the measures taken by General Hadzihasanovic at the 3rd Corps command, those for which he has been found guilty, upon being informed of the measures taken in Bugojno in response to criminal acts committed on the 5th of August. Finally, in part 4 I will address briefly the Trial Chamber's incorrect assessment, in our view, of the responsibility of General Hadzihasanovic in relation to the possibility that similar criminal acts would be committed - and here the date is important - after 18 August 1993, both in the furniture salon, as well as in other detention facilities. I now move specifically to the question posed by the Appeals Chamber. The question was: Could military disciplinary courts or superiors exercising disciplinary powers impose a sanction in excess of 60 days of imprisonment? The quick answer to the Appeals Chamber question is that military disciplinary courts or superiors exercising disciplinary powers could not impose a sanction in excess of 60 days imprisonment. However, this answer would be incomplete if I did not mention the following: Firstly, the power to impose a prison sentence of up to 60 days, as opposed to a sentence of detention - and there is a distinction and a difference - applies only to the brigade commanders and higher. This stems from the rules on military discipline, Articles 7, 8, 11, and 24, as well as from the decree law on the service in the army of the Bosnia-Herzegovina, Exhibit P120, Article 66.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please be asked to slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Will do. I apologise. A prison sentence, Mr. President, of up to 60 days, according to the rules, can only be issued in respect of breaches of discipline which are listed in Articles 7 and 8 of the rules. It should also be noted that looking at the list of breaches in Articles 7 and 8, some pursuant to the rules can also constitute criminal offences. It is not surprising then that criminal acts, such as murder or grievous bodily injury, would not be included in the listed breaches of discipline. Accordingly, it would be illegal and contrary to the rules of military discipline for a superior to use only disciplinary powers of punishment in respect of a subordinate who committed the criminal act of murder or grievous bodily injury. On the other hand, pursuant to Article 6 of the same rules, the accountability of a serviceman for a criminal offence does not exclude his being held accountable for the same offence, in relation to the same offence, for a breach of military discipline too - that's the word used in the rules - alongside, if according to these rules a military offence also constitutes a breach of military discipline. It follows that in respect of a soldier suspected of having committed the crime of murder or grievous bodily injury, for example, in addition to the applicable criminal proceedings according to the law a brigade commander could, for example, impose a prison sentence of up to 60 days imprisonment for the disciplinary breach of disobeying a lawful command or committing a criminal act for vile reasons. This is especially important in times of war where immediate response to any offence committed by a soldier is necessary. This is the best deterrent to ensure and maintain discipline, and this is in line with Article 68 of the rules, which provides that decisions on disciplinary accountability shall be taken as a matter of urgency. This was my first observation concerning the question posed by the Trial Chamber. The second observation is the following: In addition to disciplinary powers of punishment superiors had other means available to ensure that criminal acts committed by their subordinates would not go unpunished and would be treated in accordance with the law. The proper mechanism available to ensure that this would take place would be dealt with by filing and submitting a criminal report to the relevant judicial authorities. It is known and accepted in the jurisprudence of the International Tribunal that once a criminal report has been filed, the matter is in the hands of justice and the commander has fulfilled its duty -- his duty pursuant to Article 7(3) of the Statute. In this regard, I refer quickly the Appeals Chamber to the following Prosecution submission of 19 May 2004, transcript page 7704. "Once the commander has conducted an investigation and referred the matter to the relevant court authorities, his duty ends." I also refer the Appeals Chamber to the ICRC commentary of Additional Protocol 1, paragraph 3562. In closing on this specific point, Mr. President, I take the opportunity to refer the Appeals Chamber to the testimony of Sead Zeric, who was the Travnik military prosecutor at the time, regarding the manner in which a prosecutor could be seized of a case. Witness Zeric confirmed that a prosecutor could be seized of a case upon discovering -- sorry, upon receiving a criminal report. He said the criminal report can be oral or written, and he said that he could also discover the crime on his own. That was at page 5538-5539 of the transcript. Witness Zeric also confirmed that criminal reports could be filed by various bodies: By military bodies, civilian police, and by citizens directly. This is at the same pages. Witness Zeric went on to testify the following concerning the duties of prosecutors, including municipal public prosecutors, and he said that once they are seized of a criminal complaint which they feel is not within their jurisdiction, they have an obligation in this regard. Here I will quote from the transcript, lines 6 to 14 of page 5594. The question was -- or the answer was: "If a report was filed against a member of the army, every prosecutor's office is obliged to pass on the case to the competent prosecutor's office. And if it feels that it is not within a jurisdiction, it would pass it on to another prosecutor's office. So if it was filed with the basic prosecutor's office in Travnik or Bugojno" - meaning the municipal prosecutor - "and if they were army personnel, it was their obligation to pass on that case to us for further processing, and vice versa." This was not only a matter of opinion. It's also a matter of law. And I refer you to Exhibit DH337, Article 8 of the Yugoslav Law on Criminal Procedure. Finally, concerning the possibility for the military disciplinary system to work in parallel with the prosecutor's office, I would like to refer you to the testimony of the same witness regarding the practice at the time whereby a soldier would be given a disciplinary sentence or punishment while further investigations were carried out. I read from lines 13 to 20, and that is on page 5638 of the transcript: "Well, let me tell you about the practice at the time. The officer, each officer of every unit, of brigades, of corps could issue a decision on disciplinary detention for 15 or 30 days. Such was the practice. These soldiers would be detained for 15 or -- rather, for 30 days when disciplinary measures were taken against them. And during that period of time, we could carry out other investigations in order to support the detention or justify the detention of the person concerned." Although this witness referred to 30 days' detention, it is given in the rules a brigade commander could give up to 60 days' imprisonment. This concludes my part 1. I move to part 2, which deals with the nature of the measures taken in Bugojno in response to the criminal acts of 5 August in the furniture salon. To begin with, I wish to draw the attention of the facts as they were established in the trial record on the basis of the testimony of Witnesses HF, Zlotrg, Muratovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Judge Meron.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, I was very much interested in the tour de raison you made of the relevant regulations. But what would interest me is the bottom line on that. How many such criminal reports were actually filed?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: You spoke about the possibility of filing those reports. I would like to know what --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Judge, yesterday I referred the Appeals Chamber to three different exhibits. One exhibit is in -- from -- comes from Travnik, from the district military prosecutor's office, with more than 800 criminal reports. One exhibit dealt with Zenica, the Zenica District Military Court, and included more than 900 complaints. And all of these complaints, according to the evidence on the record, are -- were filed because of the policy of the 3rd Corps, because of what General Hadzihasanovic was doing; and more importantly, the evidence on the record shows that the Military Police Battalion did not let anything go unpunished on the records and at the instigation of the appellant General Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you for your question, Judge. I move on to part 2, which deals with the nature based on this law and based on those facts. And I look at the testimony of three witnesses. I said their name, HF, Zlotrg, and Muratovic, and also Exhibit P203, which is public security station information dated 20 August, and Exhibit 1392, a 3rd Corps security report dated 18 August. On the basis of this evidence, it is established firstly that the alleged perpetrators were arrested and taken into custody; secondly, that proceedings were instituted against them, DH1392; that a criminal report was filed by 307 Brigade against them, Zlotrg, 1497, corrected version; appropriate legal measures were taken in accordance with the policy of the 3rd Corps, Muratovic, 15039, corrected version; legal proceedings were underway, Muratovic, 15040, corrected version. Thirdly, it is established that after 5 August but no later than 18 August, criminal proceedings had been instigated against the perpetrators, and the municipal public prosecutor in Bugojno was seized of the matter. Exhibit P203. Fourthly, looking at the involvement of the Bugojno authorities, while the perpetrators were imprisoned, the Public Security Station, the municipal public prosecutor, the State Security Service Detachment, the security organ of the 307 Brigade, as well as the Bugojno Defence Staff were all aware of the situation and working together on this case. On the basis of these established facts, it is our submission, Mr. President, that the matter was in the hands of justice in that the municipal prosecutor was seized of the matter, and accordingly he had two options: The municipal public prosecutor could either exercise jurisdiction if he believed he had so; and to act upon it. His second choice: If he believed he did not have jurisdiction, then it was his obligation to pass on the case to the Travnik district military prosecutor, or, depending, of course, on the qualification of the crime, the crime could also go to the Zenica high public prosecutor. Consequently, it is our respectful submission that no reasonable trier of fact could conclude beyond a reasonable doubt on the basis of the evidence on the record that the measures taken in Bugojno by the 307 Brigade and all the other players I mentioned were only disciplinary in nature. It is significant in this respect that in analysing the measures taken the Trial Chamber did not refer to the involvement of the Bugojno municipal public prosecutor. At paragraphs 1771 to 1776 of the judgement, the Trial Chamber provided four reasons for its conclusion that the 3rd Corps had initiated no investigation or criminal proceedings and that the measures were only disciplinary. The Defence submits that a reasonable trier of fact could not arrive at this conclusion on the basis of the evidence referred to. It is clear, in our view, that the testimony of Muratovic taken as a whole, in light of Exhibit 1392 and in light of the testimony of Witness Zlotrg, who accompanied him in Bugojno and who is the one who drafted the Exhibit 1392, it cannot be concluded that the measures he reported to General Hadzihasanovic were solely disciplinary in nature. Secondly, regarding the testimony of Sead Zeric, the Chamber omitted in the judgement to take into consideration that this witness confirmed that he did not deal with all cases which numbered between 7 and 900 in 1993 and that he could not be sure whether he received or not a criminal report for this incident. Thirdly, the investigation conducted by Peter Hackshaw, the Defence recalls that in addition to the lack of probative value of his evidence, this witness did not go to Bugojno to search any files and there are many documents about the events in this case which we succeeded in locating on the public records: Example, in relation to Dusina - and this is documented on the record - which he did not -- or was not able to find. Lastly, regarding Witness Zrinko Alvir, the proceedings before the high court in 2004 refer to his testimony do not exclude the possibility that they were the result of the criminal proceedings which were initiated by the municipal public prosecutor in Bugojno in 1993. The statement given by this witness in 1994, when returning to Bugojno for the first time, is evidence which allows for this possibility. In any event, what is important is that the Bugojno municipal public prosecutor was seized of the matter as of 18 August at the latest and that it was his duty to act upon it or to pass on the case to the Travnik district military prosecutor. There is no evidence whatsoever on the record as to what happened after 18 August 1993, and consequently it is our submission that the Prosecution failed to prove that no measures were taken after this date. I now move to part 3 and the issue in the following section is the following: Further to the written and oral information that the appellant received. He's sitting in the 3rd Corps. He gets a visit and he gets a report. Following this information, what was his understanding of the nature of the measures taken in Bugojno in response to the acts of 5 August? Well, the evidence demonstrates that the measures taken, as we have shown, were not only disciplinary in nature. Our argument is the following: Even if they were disciplinary in nature, based on the information he received, if his understanding was that appropriate legal measures were taken in accordance with the law and if there is no specific reasons for him to question or challenge this information, then it was reasonable for him to be satisfied. And the proper conclusion is he did take necessary and reasonable measures in the circumstances ruling at the time. Looking at the reverse perspective, it would be unreasonable if this was not the case. This would impose on the commander of a corps the obligation to challenge and to investigate the measures taken in Bugojno, for example, no matter what information he received from his subordinates. Based on the evidence on the record, and including, more specifically, the testimony in the report of the defence military expert witness regarding the duties and responsibilities of a corps commander, it simply cannot be that corps commanders are expected to challenge all information they receive. Moreover, the Appeals Chamber has held, pursuant to Article 7(3), that a commander bears no responsibility for failing to obtain information from his subordinates. Celebici appeal, judgement, paragraph 226. We submit that this holding of the Appeals Chamber applies to the present scenario and that the responsibility of General Hadzihasanovic must be assessed on the basis of the information in his possession. With a view to assessing his understanding of the nature of the measures, we submit that the following must be taken into consideration: Not only the text of the written report, not only the text or the words of the testimony, but also the orders he issued concerning the prevention and punishment of criminal acts and breaches of discipline. We must bear into consideration the fact that the 3rd Corps policy in this respect had been disseminated to the Bugojno units. We must also bear -- take into consideration that the qualifications and employment of Witnesses Muratovic and Zlotrg, these two witnesses had knowledge of the related corps -- 3rd Corps policy. They knew the applicable law. They knew the rules on military discipline. And they knew the difference between the applicable procedure for breaches of discipline and those applicable to criminal acts. We must also take into consideration the duties and responsibilities of a corps commander for the detention of prisoners and related issues. Finally, then we look at the contents of the reports. Assessing the commander's understanding, in light of these considerations, leads to the following observation: First, General Hadzihasanovic could trust that 307 Brigade was informed of the difference between breaches of discipline and criminal acts and was informed of the policy of the 3rd Corps. He could trust that Muratovic and Zlotrg, working in the 3rd Corps command security sector, knew the law, knew the policy, knew the difference between criminal and disciplinary measures. And on this basis, the words they use in their written and oral reports were to be interpreted and assessed in that context. He knew that pursuant to the 3rd Corps policy measures for the repression of all breaches, whether disciplinary and/or criminal alike, would be and were taken at each level in the chain of command from the battalion, to the brigade, to the operational group, to the appellant in the 3rd Corps command. In the absence of specific information to the contrary, General Hadzihasanovic was entitled to trust that his subordinates at every level were acting in accordance with the policy. General Hadzihasanovic, as commander of a corps comprising between 30 and 40 thousand soldiers simply cannot be expected -- could not be expected to do everything himself. On this basis, we submit that the wording in the reports, both oral and written, make it clear, contrary to the Trial Chamber's conclusion, that the measures taken in Bugojno were not only disciplinary in nature.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please be asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I apologise once again. I'm sorry. The alleged perpetrators, according to the wording of the reports, were arrested, were taken into custody. Appropriate legal measures were taken in accordance with the law. Measures were taken in accordance with the policy of the 3rd Corps. And a criminal report had been filed, was being, or would be filed. The general received no report from his officers that the measures taken were insufficient. The general received no report from his officers that the measures taken in Bugojno were illegal. The general received no information from his officers which would require his immediate attention as commander of the 3rd Corps. He received no information which would create a doubt in his mind as to what took place in Bugojno. He was also aware that the information concerning this incident, based on the evidence, had been covered by three levels in the chain of command: By the brigade witness -- or not witness, but Mr. Handzic, the security officer; at the operational group level, OG Zapad, that was Dzafic, security officer for the operation group; as well as in the command itself, by Muratovic, Zlotrg, and HF. In conclusion, General Hadzihasanovic had every reason to believe in the circumstances ruling at the time that measures taken were appropriate and legal and there was no reason to believe that they were insufficient or illegal. Mr. President, even if it was the case that the Witnesses HF, Muratovic, and Zlotrg made a mistake and provided incorrect information to him, General Hadzihasanovic should not bear responsibility for that. Even if it was the case that Witness -- that Mr. Handzic, the security officer from the brigade provided wrong information to the officers which were sent to investigate, it would not be for General Hadzihasanovic to bear responsibility for that. And even if it was the case that the security level -- security officer at the operational group level, Dzafic, even if he had wrong information or if he communicated wrong information, General Hadzihasanovic should not bear responsibility for that. Consequently, the only possible conclusion is that he took -- the appellant took the necessary and reasonable measures in response to criminal acts committed by his subordinates and that the convictions for counts 3 and 4, Bugojno, must be reversed and a verdict of acquittal entered. At this point, Mr. President, I address one issue: If there is any doubt in the Appeals Chamber in respect to our arguments that he must be acquitted for these counts, then the only other option, in our view, is to order a new trial for this count. This is based on the nature and insufficiency of the measures taken in Bugojno. That's an issue which was never raised by the Trial Chamber during the testimony of Witnesses HF, Zlotrg, and Muratovic, nor under -- nor during final arguments. The nature or insufficiency of the measures was never raised by the Prosecution either at the 98 bis stage, during the testimony of these witnesses, or during the testimony of other witnesses, such as Gerritsen, or during final arguments, or in its final brief. This issue was raised proprio motu by the Trial Chamber during deliberations. The Prosecution did not meet its burden of proof in relation that these counts and there are just too many unknowns which should have been addressed by the Prosecution in the evidence. Therefore, the Trial Chamber was right in concluding that General Hadzihasanovic had knowledge -- had no evidence to show that he had knowledge of the 5 August incident and that he should have been acquitted at that time. I now refer to the -- in the judgement where the Trial Chamber says, We have no direct evidence that he was aware of the 5 August incident unless -- until the Defence witnesses came and we got those reports. That shows to us that he should have been acquitted at the end of the Prosecution's case. After the case for the Defence, if the Prosecution was surprised by the evidence that we led, by those witnesses and those documents, all the evidence that we brought forward, it could have led evidence in rebuttal, but it did not. And during the appeal, if the Prosecution was surprised with our arguments, then they could also ask for fresh evidence and do further investigations in Bugojno. They did not. The entire adjudication of this issue centres uniquely on evidence put forward by the Defence, when there was really no case to answer. For all these reasons, it would be wholly unfair in the event the a Appeals Chamber is not convinced by our arguments that he should be acquitted, to confirm this conviction without ordering a new trial on this count. I now move to part 4, the last part under counts 3 and 4, furniture salon and other detention facilities. In this part, I address briefly the Trial Chamber's guilty verdict for count 4 in relation to the period after 18 August 1993 - and the dates are very important here - for the furniture salon and for also other detention facilities in Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for the interpreters. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, Judge Shahabuddeen would like to put to you a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. -- Counsel, I read here that you are -- you have submitted that in certain circumstances you are inviting the Appeals Chamber to confirm this conviction by not ordering a new trial on this count; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That's incorrect, Mr. -- Incorrect, Judge. They're both -- both are to be looked in the opposite way. We want to reverse the conviction and that conviction should not stand. If you have any idea or any doubt into -- in your mind as to not reversing the count, then we say we need a new trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Because of what happened. Thank you, Judge. The last part of my argument deals with the period after 18 August. I'd like to come back on this to paragraph 251 of the appeal brief, which clearly highlights the unreasonable character of the Trial Chamber's verdicts. The rationale behind the Trial Chamber's verdict is that because Hadzihasanovic failed to take appropriate measures in respect of the 5 August incident, then he had reason to know that the commission of similar illicit acts after 18 August was a real and reasonable risk. And accordingly, the Trial Chamber says he created a situation conducive to the repetition of similar criminal acts after 18 August, not only at the furniture salon but also at other detention facilities. The furniture salon, Mr. President, dear Judges, was never mentioned in any report to General Hadzihasanovic. What was reported to him was a situation involving two soldiers who had beaten up HVO prisoners. Secondly, the Trial Chamber found that General Hadzihasanovic - and here it's very important - did not have knowledge of the poor detention conditions whether at the furniture salon or at the other detention facilities. Then comes some crucial findings of the Trial Chamber at paragraphs 1759, 60, 61, 83, 84, and 85. In these paragraphs, the Trial Chamber established the following: General Hadzihasanovic did not have any alarming information that would have warned him that similar criminal acts had been committed by soldiers of 307 Brigade at other detention centres in Bugojno. Secondly, when he learned of the 5 August incident, the Trial Chamber states he did not have reason to know that his subordinates had committed other crimes of mistreatment, whether at the furniture salon or at other detention facilities. The information communicated to General Hadzihasanovic did not reveal, according to the Trial Chamber, a repeated practice of mistreatment but, rather, one incident which had taken place on one occasion, on 5 August 1993. The information communicated to General Hadzihasanovic was not enough for him to believe, according to the Trial Chamber - that's very important - that this incident was preceded or followed by other criminal acts of the same nature. In other words, this is what the Trial Chamber concluded: One, there was a serious incident on 5 August; two, there were no similar incidents before 5 August; three, there were no similar incidents during the period between 5 August and 18 August. Consequently, it is our submission that no reasonable trier of law and fact - because we believe that this is a misapplication of Article 7(3) mens rea - could conclude that General Hadzihasanovic had reason to know that his subordinates were about to commit similar criminal acts at any of the detention facilities in Bugojno. It follows that the conviction entered for count 4, in respect of potential cruel treatment after 18 August at the furniture salon, the Gimnazija, the FC Iskra Stadium, and the Vojin Paleksic school, must be reversed. In relation to all the other issues raised in relation to the third ground of appeal, we stand by our submissions. And I move to the fifth ground, Orasac. The events, Mr. President, which took place in Orasac deal specifically, as you know, with the actions of the so-called Mujahedin, or El Mujahid Detachment, the main issue being whether a superior-to-subordinate relationship existed between General Hadzihasanovic, as commander of the 3rd Corps, and these forces. Our fifth ground of appeal on this topic comprises no less than seven sub-grounds of appeal. Each of those is, in our view, part of a logical sequence, from the issue of control to the issue of measures. At the same time, each of these grounds is a stand-alone and only one needs to be successful, in our submission, to justify the reversals of the conviction entered by the Trial Chamber for counts 3 and 4, Orasac. My submissions will be divided in three parts -- or three sections.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please be asked to slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Once again, I apologise. I'm doing my best. In section 1, I will respond to the question posed by the Appeals Chamber to the Prosecution in the Scheduling Order. In section 2, I will address in some detail our first and sixth sub-grounds of appeal. And then these grounds deal with the issue of the use of force by a commander against his own subordinates and the sixth sub-ground deals with the criteria which must be fulfilled for effective control to exist if the Appeals Chamber comes to the conclusion that this is included in his material ability to prevent or punish. Finally, in section 3, I will address the remaining five sub-grounds, focusing on a few important issues in each case. The question put to the Prosecution in the Scheduling Order is divided in two parts. First, to point the evidence in the trial record pertaining to the failure of General Hadzihasanovic to provide Mujahedin with international humanitarian law - which I will refer to as IHL - training and to set up a disciplinary system to ensure compliance with the Rules. Secondly, to explain whether such failure would be sufficient in itself for General Hadzihasanovic to incur criminal responsibility for failure to prevent the crimes of cruel treatment and the crime of murder of Dragan Popovic. I'll answer these questions in the reverse order. First, it is our submission that failure to provide the Mujahedin with IHL training and to set up a disciplinary system is not sufficiently in itself for the appellant to incur criminal responsibility for failure to prevent cruel treatment and murder of Popovic. Failure to provide IHL training and to set up a disciplinary system only becomes relevant, moreover, in the presence of a superior-to-subordinate relationship between the commander and the group concerned. If General Hadzihasanovic did not exercise effective control over Mujahedin, then the issue is moot. Secondly, it is our submission that providing IHL training and setting up a disciplinary system are included in the responsibilities and duties of a commander from the moment he assumes command. These duties and responsibilities are a standing obligation for the commander pursuant to customary international law, even if he does not have reason to know that a subordinate is committing or is about to commit a crime. This is something he does at all times. In this case, Mr. President, we have never undermined the importance of the duties and responsibilities of a corps commander. On the contrary, we have proven in many respects that he was a good commander and that he did fulfil his responsibilities and obligations. These responsibilities, Mr. President, are, in our view, part of his general duty of prevention, as well as to his duty to ensure that subordinates will comply with the dictates of IHL. This is different from the commander's duty if he knows or had reason to know that a subordinate was committing or about to commit a crime. Then he must take necessary and reasonable measures to prevent this crime. The difference between the two is supported by the fact that if the crime is committed or about to be committed, it is very unlikely at this point that training in IHL will be sufficient to prevent this crime from happening. Consequently, while the commander who fails to train subordinates or to set up a disciplinary system is certainly in breach of his general duty of prevention, providing, of course, that he was able to do so, this is insufficient to attract criminal responsibility for a crime committed by a subordinate. In other words, his responsibility for a crime committed by a subordinate will be and must be assessed on the measures he took once he knew or had reason to know that the crime was being committed or about to be committed. Looking at the same situation from the reverse perspective, a commander who failed to take necessary and reasonable measures to prevent a crime by a subordinate, in our -- in our submission, could not say -- could not say, I'm not guilty, because I provided IHL training to my troops before I ever had any reason to know about the crime which was being committed or about to be committed. Finally, a further argument is that even though providing IHL training to subordinates and setting up a disciplinary system is included in the responsibilities of a commander, pursuant to Article 87 of Additional Protocol 1, failure to do so is not a breach which attracts criminal responsibility in relation to a crime which had been committed by a subordinate as, for example, in Article 86 of Additional Protocol 1. In response to the second part of the question, a comprehensive review of the evidence of the trial record reveals, in our respectful submission, that both issues, failure to provide IHL training to Mujahedin, and failure to set up a disciplinary system for Mujahedin, were not addressed, whether in witness testimony or documentary evidence. This is in fact confirmed by the Trial Chamber at paragraphs 1434 of the judgement. On the other hand, the trial record is replete with examples of the numerous measures taken by General Hadzihasanovic to stress, amongst other things, the importance of training for his troops, to distribute Geneva Conventions to his troops, to draw their attention to the obligations they entail, to instruct his officers concerning their legal obligations, and to train his troops in military discipline. If General Hadzihasanovic did this for the units under his command, the question becomes: Why then would he not do so for Mujahedin if they were under his command? The evidence is silent on this question. I turn to section 2 of my submission, which addresses the first and sixth ground of appeal, six sub-grounds. It is our submission, Mr. President, that the obligation for a commander to use military force against a group of fighters --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, I would like to stay for a moment on this question of the authority of Mr. Hadzihasanovic over the Mujahedin. And there are, of course, legally, two questions there. The first one is the question of de jure superior relationship between the 3rd Corps and the Mujahedin. And the second question is the question of effective control. Do I understand you to argue that there was no de jure authority and no de facto authority?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: This is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Both of these.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: This is exactly the case, Judge. We argue that there is a mistake which led to an error on the part of the Trial Chamber about de jure control, which we say never existed; sub-ground of appeal 2. And that the effective control never existed; sub-ground of appeal 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: You are, of course, aware of the fact that the trial judgement in paragraph 853, I believe, reached the conclusion that there was effective control over the Mujahedin. Would you say that no reasonable trier of fact could have reached the conclusion that Hadzihasanovic had de facto control over the Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Absolutely, Judge. And later on in my argument I will refer to the holdings of the Appeals Chamber in the Blaskic case. And I will say if we look at the facts in this case and the way the Appeals Chamber applied the effective control test in the Blaskic case or in the Blaskic appeal, then there is absolutely no way that the relationship which existed between General Hadzihasanovic and the Mujahedin can be even considered to come close to effective control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: So we will be returning to this point, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Absolutely, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: My second question - and I don't know whether this is the best time to ask you that, but I would not mind if you would return to it later on - you mentioned in your argument today the had-reason-to-know test. And you, of course, know that this test draws importantly on the Krnojelac appeals decision. If the Trial Chamber applied that test, had-reason-to-know, in an impermissible fashion, I would like you at one point during your argument to point specifically to parts of the judgements which would be invalidated as a result of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. Did I understand Krnojelac judgement from the from the Appeals Chamber? It is our submission, Judge, that if the Appeals Chamber follows the same route with the had-reason-to-know, it would find that there is no had-reason-to-know in the previous circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: No, I understand that. But what I meant is do you argue that the standard of Krnojelac was incorrectly applied?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That's exactly the case. We feel that the -- the Trial Chamber in the judgement went over the Krnojelac judgement and decided to depart from the Appeals Chamber holdings, whereas the Appeals Chamber had conducted a very detailed review of the circumstances involving Mr. Krnojelac, the fact that he was at the prison, that he saw beatings that -- and all the facts surrounding his situation. The Appeals Chamber conducted that on the whole he had such alarming information that he had reason to know. The Trial Chamber, on the other hand, went to say that if -- if the general knows that in the same brigade in the same general geographical area a crime was committed, it has reason to know about all the other crimes committed by the same brigade in the same area, he has reason to know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And we believe that this is wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: And if this standard was impermissibly applied --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: -- which parts of the judgement would be affected by that? Could you tell us that during the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, Judges, the part that I referred to earlier on. It's the conclusions that if -- if the Trial Chamber says: One incident, 5 August, nothing happened before, nothing happened between 5 and 18 but then there's suddenly had-reason-to-know that pops up on the 18th. For us, that's where it went wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Judge Liu.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have just a follow-up question with Judge Meron's question concerning with the effective control. I would like to know, was your position on Mr. Hadzihasanovic's material ability to prevent or punish the members of the Mujahedin at that moment? You may answer this question now, but if you come across this question at a later stage, I could wait.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Judge. This is exactly the point I'm addressing now. And we feel there are two ways to address this question in our arguments. We have a detailed ground of appeal, which we say, had the Trial Chamber correctly analysed all the evidence on the record, then it would come to the conclusion that there was no material ability to prevent or punish. But for now I want to address the Trial Chamber's own finding, which makes that, in our view, very clear. And that is the fact that the Trial Chamber said that a commander, as part of his material ability to punish, is in a position where he must use force to do so. So the Trial Chamber included the use of military assets and attacking subordinates as a manner to apply effective control. In our view, this makes no sense. And this is what I get into at this part. The importance of this issue stems from the Trial Chamber's finding at paragraph 1459, which reads as follows: "The only way in which the 3rd Corps could deal with the situation it faced was to use military assets against the El Mujahedin Detachment immediately." The situation in this quote refers to the seriousness of offences which took place, to the fact that past threats to use force had not had the deterrent effect counted on, on the lack of discipline shown by the El Mujahid Detachment, and by the fact that initiating talks at that stage was useless. These are all Trial Chamber conclusions. We respectfully submit that this finding most accurately reflects the totality of the evidence on the record concerning the state of affairs related to Mujahedin during the period from August to December 1993. It shows, in our view, that the Mujahedins were uncontrolled elements which did not accept to be under command and control of the 3rd Corps. Strikingly, the Prosecutor has not addressed this specific finding of the Trial Chamber in its response, which, in our view, is revealing. On the basis of this finding, we submit that in such a situation a superior-to-subordinate relationship in the sense of Article 7(3) cannot be said to exist. If a group of fighters refuses to carry out the orders of a commander and the only way to bring them into submission is to use military force and to attack them, surely it cannot be said that this commander exercises effective control over this group. The question at this stage is whether or not -- is not whether or not the commander is able to use force to attack the group. It is, rather, whether the commander has the material ability to prevent or punish --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please be asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Will do. Thank you. So the question, Mr. President, is not whether he has the material assets to attack; the question is whether he has the material ability to prevent or punish acts committed by this group which refuses to obey his order. To us, there's no confusion, contrary to the Prosecution argument, between the first and third elements of command responsibility. The meaning of effective control --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Judge Shahabuddeen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, I understand your proposition that the issue turns on proof of effective control. Well, is there a principle in military organisations which says that a military commander in a given sector has to have control of all personnel in that area? In other words, is there a principle of unity of --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your question, Judge. To me the answer is very simple.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In times of occupation, a commander may have some kind of a geographical responsibility for what happens in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If it's not times of occupation, that simply is not the case. The military commander is only responsible for everything that is -- his soldiers do. And that's effective control. No effective control, no responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber's analysis, the meaning of effective control, as I was saying, is well-defined in the jurisprudence of the International Tribunal. It is our submission that the use of military force to attack a group who will not carry out orders is at odds with this concept as set out in our military pleadings -- in our written pleadings. Sorry. The Trial Chamber's analysis of the issue at paragraphs 85 to 87, without providing any authority for -- in support, is both important and revealing. With all due respect for the Trial Chamber, I believe it may -- it may have confused the following two terms: "Material ability to prevent or punish," as defined in the jurisprudence of the International Tribunal with "the possession of military assets and the possibility to use them" because of the French definition, "capacite materielle de faire usage de la force," which is a different concept altogether. In this regard, we disagree with the last sentence of paragraph 86 of the judgement, which must be looked at, in our view, by the Appeals Chamber. In our view, the only situation in which a commander may be compelled to use force to enforce international humanitarian law is when the use of force is required against the enemy as a means of reprisal, not in the context referred to by the -- by the Trial Chamber. We also disagree with the second sentence of paragraph 87 of the judgement that because orders must be obeyed for an army to function - everybody agrees with that - a commander would not hesitate to use force in cases where they refused to obey a combat order. This simply cannot be the case, Mr. President. Moreover, the same reasoning applies to the third sentence, where the only occasion, in our respectful opinion, a commander may find himself in a position where he must order the execution of a soldier who refuses to obey his orders is when this soldier was tried and convicted in accordance with applicable international norms. It simply cannot be the case that a commander -- You refuse to obey my order; I shoot you. That's my reading of the trial judgement. I may be wrong. But I think the Appeals Chamber must look at such holdings in the trial judgement. In the end, Mr. President, perhaps there is a situation when a commander may be compelled to use force against his subordinates. That is, if they join the enemy and they begin firing at his unit. But then again, they are no longer subordinates; they are former subordinates. While these conclusions of the Trial Chamber may explain the finding that General Hadzihasanovic exercise effective control over Mujahedin, even though the only way for him was to attack them, we respectfully believe that this finding which is contrary to the jurisprudence of the International Tribunal, cannot stand. I referred you earlier to the case of Blaskic, which was adjudicated by the Appeals Chamber. In that case, the Appeals Chamber held that Blaskic did not exercise effective control over the 4 Military Police Battalion, concerning the HVO attack on Ahmici, even though the 4 Military Police Battalion was a regular HVO unit, was present and included in the Central Bosnia operative zone, which was under the command of Colonel Blaskic, and this 4 Military Police Battalion could be attached to him for ad hoc missions pursuant to specific requests. Despite all this, the Appeals Chamber said, no effective control. Our submission is, when we compare the facts of both cases, the situation prevailing at the time between the commander of the 3rd Corps and the Mujahedin does not even come close to the kind of relationship which existed between Blaskic and the 4 Military Police Battalion. In these circumstances, we take the view that our first sub-ground of appeal must succeed and we respectfully request that the convictions entered against General Hadzihasanovic for counts 3 and 4, Mujahedin and Orasac, be reversed and a verdict of acquittal entered. I now move on to our sixth sub-ground of appeal set out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Counsel, can you try to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Will do, Mr. President. I'm looking at the time and I'm ... The sixth sub-ground of appeal is set out in paragraphs 371 and 373 of the appellant brief. In the event the Appeals Chamber disagrees with our submission on the previous issue, that is, if the Appeals Chamber holds that use of military assets and attacking subordinates in order as a means to prevent and punish, then and only then our sixth sub-ground of appeal becomes relevant. If it's the fact that having to attack a subordinate does not automatically negate any effective control the commander exercises over his troops, then, in our view, it must still fulfil the criteria had the material ability to prevent or punish. And in such a case, this would require three criteria to be -- to be fulfilled. In other words, we submit that if the use of force and military assets, which we say is not, is included in the material ability to prevent or punish, then the commander will only have effective control if he has the legal authority under domestic law to attack his subordinates; if he has the necessary military authority; and if he possesses the military assets necessary to launch such an attack. In respect of these submissions, we refer the Appeals Chamber to our written pleadings in paragraphs 373 to 394.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Judge Guney would like to put a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon, there is the -- the exercise of the authority of effective control, but there's also the de jure control. That's on the one hand. And then also there is the material capability to prevent and punish. Is it possible to have the material capacity to prevent and punish without having effective control, be it that or the de jure control? So I'd like to know your view on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. The answer is very simple: The Appeals Chamber clearly established that for a commander to have the material capability -- or ability to prevent or punish, he must exert effective control. But the relationship between effective and de jure control, in both cases you must have evidence of effective control [In English] to prevent and punish. An effective control to prevent and punish includes or has been defined as the material ability to prevent and punish. And the material ability to prevent and punish, if that is not there, then this is the end of the matter. You need either de jure or effective control. But even with de jure, this would not be sufficient, according to our submissions and the holdings of the Appeals Chamber. I now move to simply my conclusion, and that is that whether the Appeals Chamber adopts the position where using military assets and attacking does not negate effective control. And if you look at it the other way, the criteria I have just mentioned, domestic legal authority and military authority and possession of military assets is not there. Is simply, it cannot be that the Trial Chamber would find, that a reasonable -- a reasonable trier of fact would find the material ability to prevent or punish. I now move quickly to some of our arguments in grounds 2 to 5. In our view, these are determining arguments which can facilitate adjudication by the Appeals Chamber. With respect to sub-ground 2, we maintain, as set out in our written pleadings, that the Trial Chamber committed numerous incorrect conclusions of facts which have occasioned a miscarriage of justice. It is our submission that no reasonable trier of fact could have concluded on its analysis of the evidence on the record that the Mujahedin were under de jure command of the 3rd Corps. Considering that this sub-ground deals with de jure -- and specifically with de jure control, we submit that the testimony of Poparic was especially important and respectfully submit that the Trial Chamber was incorrect in setting it aside as being an administrative matter. As for the documents involved or used by the Trial Chamber - namely, some orders and letters - it is significant that the sole document amongst these six letters and orders is the 28 August 1993 order which bears the mention "not carried out." The related testimony of Kulenovic at pages 13953 and 13961 is also important in respect of these documents. Finally, the incorrect inference drawn by the Trial Chamber from what we say is -- was an unreliable, even totally unreliable Mujahedin propaganda video, the Trial Chamber drew an inference concerning the existence of an agreement between the Mujahedin and the Bosnian army leadership which was incorrect. Moving on to the sub-ground 3. We submit, as set out in our written pleadings, that the Trial Chamber -- or that no reasonable trier of fact could have concluded from its analysis of the evidence on the record that the Mujahedin were under effective control of the 3rd Corps. In addition to the fact that a large amount of evidence, which, in our view, has high probative value, was not attributed any weight, as described in our pleadings, we invite the Trial -- the Appeals Chamber to take a close look at the analysis of effective control which was performed by the Trial Chamber for the period before 13 August 1993 and after 13 August 1993. In this regard, over and above the fact that the Trial Chamber, we say, incorrectly attributed weight to unreliable evidence for the period after 13 August 1993 - and I refer here to the Mujahedin propaganda video, P482, as well as to the war diaries and operational logbooks, C11 to C20 - in our view, it stands from the evidence on the record that other than that the Delic order of 13 August 1993, which was used as a separation point by the Trial Chamber and for which there is no response on the record, nothing had really changed regarding the lack of effective control over the Mujahedin after 13 August. One of the Trial Chamber's errors, in our submission - this one was conceded by the Prosecution in its response at paragraph 257 - has special importance: That is, the conclusion that members of Mujahedin were in fact tried by the municipal court in Travnik and not, as the Trial Chamber held, by the district military court. Another of the Trial Chamber's errors, which we say has significant importance, is the incorrect inference which was drawn from the war diaries C11 and C13 for 7 September 1993. Contrary to the Trial Chamber's finding, these entries do not show that the Mujahedin participated in combat activities at the request of 325 Brigade. On that occasion, 325 Brigade was in fact assisted by the Military Police Battalion -- or Military Police Platoon of operational group Bosanska Krajina, OG BK, and 27 Brigade. I move to the fourth sub-ground, which deals with the had-reason-to-know criteria. It is our submission that no reasonable trier of fact could conclude that General Hadzihasanovic had knowledge of the abduction of five Croat civilians in Travnik of 20 October 1993. The Trial Chamber started its analysis from the absence of evidence, establishing direct knowledge. Then the Trial Chamber went on, in our respectful view, to search and to find on the basis of a series of unverified deductions and assumptions that General Hadzihasanovic had knowledge. I thought there was a question. It is important to note what the Trial Chamber held. It held all of the following on the basis of a few pieces of evidence: It held that General Hadzihasanovic knew that five civilians were abducted by Mujahedin on 19 October; that he knew what measures and steps had already been taken by Operational Group Bosanska Krajina, OG BK, to resolve the crisis; that he knew that in response to threats by one Mujahedin, Alagic, the commander of OG BK, had forbidden Mujahedin to abduct civilians. That he knew that despite these threats a first group of five civilians was kidnapped on 16 October; that he knew that following the first abductions, OG BK had threatened the Mujahedin that they would attack them. All of these findings, everything I've just mentioned, was established entirely on the basis of constructive knowledge. In our submission, one of the incorrect inferences by the Trial Chamber in this regard tells it all. Contrary to the Trial Chamber's finding, the support received from the corps commander mentioned by Witness HE referred to, in fact, to the situation after he learned about the killing of Popovic in early November 1993. At that time, Alagic was the new commander of the 3rd Corps and not Hadzihasanovic. You take this part out of the equation, and in our view, the playing cards castle falls apart. Moving to the fifth sub-ground of appeal set out in paragraph 360. It is our submission that the Trial Chamber erred in law by concluding at paragraphs 1463 and 1465 that there exist an implicit causal link between the failure to act to prevent a crime and the commission of that crime and that such an implicit causal link could be presumed. In our respectful submission, this is straightforward contrary to the jurisprudence of the International Tribunal. We only mention this at this time to highlight the fact that, in our respectful submission, the aim of the Trial Chamber in finding the existence of such a causal link was to shift the burden on the accused to prove the feasibility of the measures which he should have used. Consequently, we take the view that this error of law invalidates the trial's analysis of the measures which, in its view, should have been taken by General Hadzihasanovic. Mr. President, I note I have ten minutes left, according to my legal assistant. Would you like to take the break now and give me ten minutes at the end or to -- for me to conclude in ten minutes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I believe I prefer you conclude in ten minutes now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. It is our submission with respect to the final sub-ground at paragraphs 395 to 407 that no reasonable trier of fact, having properly assessed the evidence on the record, could conclude that launching an attack against the El Mujahid Detachment, with a view to securing the release of five civilians kidnapped by the Mujahedin, was a necessary and reasonable measure in the circumstances ruling at the time. In this regard, the only point we'd like to raise relates to the issues which were not addressed by the Trial Chamber in its analysis as to whether or not launching an attack against the Mujahedin was a necessary and reasonable measure. These issues include the impact of the attack on the accomplishment of the mission, the likely collateral damage, the chances of success of the attack, and the rule of proportionality. We note in this regard that the Prosecution did not even attempt to address these criteria, but it's not surprising --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please kindly slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: They did not even enter into this area. And in our view, the Appeals Chamber does not need to do so either because it will be determined from the get-go that there was no effective control. In light of all these submissions, Mr. President, we respectfully request the convictions entered against General Hadzihasanovic for counts 3 and 4, Mujahedin and Orasac, to be reversed and a verdict of acquittal entered. Finally, in my last minutes I move to the fourth ground of appeal, related to music school. And I refer the Appeals Chamber to paragraph 409 to 483 in the appeals brief. It is our submission that no necessary -- no reasonable trier of fact could conclude that General Hadzihasanovic failed in his duty as a superior to take the necessary and reasonable measures to punish the perpetrators and to prevent treatment at the music school, and very importantly, in the circumstances ruling at the time. The Trial Chamber, firstly, erred in the disposition of the judgement, which does not reflect its findings. Also, the Trial Chamber erred by failing to properly consider and attach probative value to the evidence provided by Witness Merdan and HF concerning their investigation of the situation at the music school when necessary. I mentioned at the beginning that this ground only deals with cruel treatment and there was no murder. Nobody died in the music school, and only cruel treatment. Witness Merdan was the deputy commander of the 3rd Corps, a witness who has testified in many cases before this Tribunal. He testified for many days, during which he was extensively questioned by the Trial Chamber. There was no objective reason, in our view, for the Trial Chamber to set aside his testimony as it did. This relates to a further ground of appeal. We would have liked to hear Witness Merdan here again if the Appeals Chamber had any doubt. It was decided not to call him again to testify, but we do feel that his testimony must bear close scrutiny by the Appeals Chamber. Thirdly, the Trial Chamber erred by failing to consider and attach probative value to the evidence related to the fact that both the detention and the mistreatment of prisoners was voluntarily concealed from the 3rd Corps command. And lastly, it is our submission that the evaluation of the evidence on the record was incorrect because the situation was not appreciated on the basis of in the circumstances ruling at the time, and also from the perspective of the appellant, as commander of a corps, in the circumstances. This brings us to two conclusions. It stems from the evidence that the detention and mistreatment of prisoners was concealed from the 3rd Corps. Nonetheless, that General Hadzihasanovic was put on notice of the possibility that prisoners were detained. On those occasions, General Hadzihasanovic investigated the matter, sending his most serious officers to investigate. The reality of what was happening at the music school at the time was unfortunately not uncovered. On this basis, no reasonable trier of fact could be satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that the appellant failed to take necessary and reasonable measures. Such a conclusion would be entirely inconsistent with the evidence on the record concerning the manner in which General Hadzihasanovic exercised his command. Consequently, the Defence respectfully requests the Appeals Chamber to overturn the judgement and return a verdict of not guilty for count 4, failure to punish, cruel treatment at the music school. And this puts an end to my submissions, Mr. President. If you have any questions, I will be glad to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Any questions from the Bench? No, that's not the case. So we can break now for 20 minutes, as in the schedule, and reconvene at 10.20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Well, I give now the floor to the Prosecution for their submissions. Please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Before beginning with the Prosecution's response, we need to correct one error in yesterday's submissions regarding the sentence of Hadzihasanovic. When addressing the gravity of the crime, I referred to Witness ZH's experience of being beaten at his arrival in the Gimnazija school. That is transcript page 68, line 19 and following. While this event on the 23rd of July, 1993 falls within the time frame set out in the disposition, in its brief the Prosecution agreed that the disposition is incorrect and should read 18 August to 8 October 1993. Therefore, the beating of ZH on 23 July is not something we ask you to take into account when assessing the gravity. However, the Trial Chamber also found that the same witness, ZH, suffered further beating of a similar nature on the 17th of September within the time period. That is trial judgement, paragraph 1665. We ask Your Honours to take that into account. And in 1666, the Trial Chamber sets out the injuries resulting from the treatment at the Gimnazija school. I will now -- we will now proceed with our response. I will first deal with question 1 Your Honours have asked, and then address the ground relating to Bugojno. Mr. Kremer will after that address the ground relating to Orasac. And after that, Mr. Tracol will address the Zenica music school. Regarding the first question, Your Honours have asked whether based on the rules of military discipline or any other relevant provision, could military disciplinary courts or superiors exercising disciplinary powers impose a sanction in excess of 60 days imprisonment. We agree with the Defence that the answer is "no," both military disciplinary courts and military superiors, the highest punishment for them was 60 days imprisonment. The sanctioning powers are regulated in Article 11 of rules on military discipline, P325, read together with Article 66 of the decree law on service in the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, P120. Article 11 provides that for the errors of discipline and military infractions, disciplinary measures and disciplinary punishment stipulated in Article 66 of the decree law on service in the armed forces may be imposed. And Article 65 of the decree distinguishes between an error of discipline, the minor breach, and the disciplinary offence, the severe breach. And according sanctions are then listed in Article 66, for which then the minor breaches and the major breaches have as the maximum punishment 60 days' imprisonment. The organ in charge of imposing the punishment is again set out in the rules of military discipline, Exhibit P325. Under these rules, the military superiors shall have the authority to establish responsibility for the minor offence, the errors of discipline, Article 22; and the military courts have the authority to try the major ones, the military infractions, Article 44. This answers -- this is our submission to the question. And unless Your Honours have questions regarding this, I would move on to our response to the ground of appeal regarding Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: With regard to the ground relating to Bugojno, I will first address the measures that were taken at Bugojno and the awareness of General Hadzihasanovic of the kind of measures taken, and will then move to his mens rea regarding the failure to prevent of future crimes. With regard to the measures taken, Hadzihasanovic failed to show that it was unreasonable for the Trial Chamber to conclude, first, that the measures taken against the perpetrators of cruel treatment and murder on 5 August were only disciplinary; and second, had -- that Hadzihasanovic was only informed about disciplinary measures and expressed his satisfaction in this regard. The Trial Chamber carefully analysed the evidence of the types of measures taken, referring to one exhibit, the inspection report, 13 -- DH1392, and the testimony of six witnesses, Witness Muratovic, Zlotrg, HF, Zeric, Hackshaw, and Alvir, and it reached a conclusion that was not unreasonable. Hadzihasanovic now raises concerns with regard to the translation of two testimonies, the one of Muratovic and Zlotrg, but our position is that the change between the English and French transcript and the official translation does not render the Trial Chamber's ultimate conclusion unreasonable. The Trial Chamber first concluded that neither the inspection report nor the testimony of Witness HF made it explicit what kind of measures were taken. And regarding Witness Zlotrg, the Trial Chamber finds in paragraph 1768 that he seems to indicate that the actions taken were criminal in nature and the official translation makes clear that he talks about a criminal report which, according to transcript page 1946 in the official version, has -- had been filed and which, according to his testimony in cross-examination on transcript page 14999, was going to be filed. But in any event, Hadzihasanovic still failed to show that it was unreasonable for the Trial Chamber to conclude, despite this testimony, that measures taken were only disciplinary, in light of the other evidence looked at. The Trial Chamber next looked at the testimony of Muratovic and concluded that he specified that the measures were disciplinary in nature. The -- even the change of his testimony through the revised translation does not reveal that he talks about a criminal report being filed or criminal measures being taken. The only thing he says is that "We received an oral report when we were in Bugojno and were told that legal proceedings were underway." But we say it's reasonable for the Trial Chamber to conclude that he was not talking about two things, disciplinary proceedings and criminal proceedings, but only about disciplinary proceedings, in light of the fact that when he was asked, "Are you aware that a trial was ever conducted," he said, "They were brought before the military disciplinary organ in Bugojno and were punished." Therefore, it's reasonable for the Trial Chamber to conclude that he was only talking about disciplinary measures. Particularly, it cannot be argued that the ultimate conclusion that only disciplinary measures were taken was one which no reasonable Trial Chamber could reach, taking into account the other three witnesses the Trial Chamber relied upon, Witness Alvir and particularly Witness Hackshaw, whom the Trial Chamber trusted with regard to murder - that is paragraph 994 of the judgement - and Witness Zeric. The Trial Chamber was entitled to put particular weight to the clear evidence of Witness Zeric, the Travnik military prosecutor, during the period the crimes were committed until February 1996. He gave a clear answer on transcript page 5528 when asked, "Can you recall any reports that you received in respect of ABiH soldiers killing prisoners of war or any prisoners at all?" Answer: "We never received any such report." Question: "Did you receive any report alleging that ABiH soldiers mistreated HVO prisoners of war?" Answer: "I never received any such report." Hadzihasanovic also mentioned that the evidence that a criminal report was filed is contained in Exhibit P -- P203. The Trial Chamber does not refer to this exhibit in this particular section of the judgement, but it was well aware of it. It referred to it in several other parts of the judgement, such as paragraph 1646 and 1671, and the Trial Chamber does not have to refer to every piece of evidence as set out in the Kupreskic appeal judgement, paragraph 293. Regarding the content of Exhibit P203, it is a report dated 20 August 1993 which Senad Dautovic, the chief of the civilian police in Bugojno sent inter alia to the 307th Brigade and relates to a meeting attended by the municipal prosecutor and the European Community observers. And the exhibit says that criminal proceedings had been instituted against those who committed the crime and the annex refers to the murder of Mladen Havranek, but it also says that the individuals had been punished. Moreover, the Defence mentioned that since the military prosecutor had attended the meeting, he would have either dealt with the matter himself or sent it to the military prosecutor. However, the municipal prosecutor is only competent, according to paragraph 1 -- 9 -- paragraph 954 of the judgement, to deal with matters regarding civilians or when civilians were co-perpetrators with military officials, but here the Trial Chamber found that the perpetrators were members of the 307th Brigade. Therefore, he was not competent and would have to refer the matter to the military prosecutor, who gave clear evidence that he had never received such a report. Consequently, the Trial Chamber's conclusion that no military report was filed is a reasonable conclusion. With regard to what Hadzihasanovic knew about the measures taken, the trial judgement refers to the inspection report, which was addressed to the 3rd Corps, but this report does not provide specific information about the types of measures taken. It just says proceedings were instituted. And the Trial Chamber, moreover, describes the conversation between Muratovic and Hadzihasanovic, and Muratovic even in the official corrected version does not talk about criminal measures being taken or a criminal report being filed; he just talks about the appropriate legal measures were taken, in accordance with the law. From our point of view, therefore, it was not unreasonable for the Trial Chamber to conclude that Hadzihasanovic was merely informed about disciplinary measures. This ends my submission on the measures taken and Hadzihasanovic's knowledge thereof. And if Your Honours have no further questions, I would move on to his mens rea regarding future crimes. We have set out in our response brief, that the Trial Chamber did not commit an error with its legal test that the awareness of a real and reasonable risk is the correct mens rea standard, and I would now like to address the factual question whether the fact that Hadzihasanovic was aware of one serious incident of cruel treatment of six and the murder of one prisoner of war in the furniture salon is sufficient to trigger his awareness of a real and reasonable risk of other crimes, future crimes, in the furniture salon, as well as in other detention facilities in Bugojno, especially when coupled with the failure to take adequate measures to punish the incident. The answer is "yes," especially in light of the inadequate measures taken. Not only did Hadzihasanovic know of the incident of cruel treatment and murder; he also failed to adequately punish. The Krnojelac appeals judgement supports this proposition. The Krnojelac judgement endorses the notion that the awareness of one incident may be sufficient to trigger had-reason-to-know. The Appeals Chamber holds in paragraph 169 that while the fact that Krnojelac witnessed the torture inflicted on one detainee is not sufficient to constitute that he knew that future crimes would happen, but it says it may nevertheless constitute sufficiently alarming information as to alert him of the risk of other acts of torture being committed. In other words, Krnojelac's awareness that one detainee was tortured may have been sufficient to give him reason to know that his subordinates were committing or were about to commit acts of torture against other detainees. By contrast, the Trial Chamber seems to require in paragraph 1760 a situation of recurrent criminal acts to trigger the had-reason-to-know, that the awareness of one incident is sufficient is also supported by the Rauer case referred to by the Trial Chamber in paragraph 165, especially the case note supports the proposition that after becoming aware of one incident, Rauer he had a legal duty to take measures to prevent repetition. Moreover, failure to take adequate measures to punish has an encouraging effect, which means that the risk of future crimes is higher; therefore, also the awareness of the risk increases. Failure to punish has an implicit encouraging effect because the subordinates believe that they can commit further crimes with impunity. That is supported by the Celebici appeal judgement, para 739. The same can be said, albeit to a lesser extent, with regard to the failure to take appropriate measures, especially taking into account the obvious discrepancy in punishment, maximum of 60 days for disciplinary sanction and the minimum of five years for war crimes under the SFRY Criminal Code. In other words, if a superior takes inadequate measures, this can still have an encouraging effect. Therefore, Hadzihasanovic, by being aware of one serious incident, plus his failure to take the adequate measures, had reason to know that future crimes would be committed in the furniture salon and other detention facilities in Bugojno which had the same group of people and were in close geographic proximity. This ends my submission on Bugojno, and unless Your Honours have questions, I would pass on to Mr. Kremer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Your Honours, let me begin the submissions on Orasac by, first of all, pointing out that there is an error in the disposition. The disposition refers to a period from the 15th of October to the 31st of October, 1993. The proper disposition should have been, according to the findings in the judgement, from the 19th of October to the 31st of October, when the second group of Croat civilians was abducted by the members of the El Mujahedin Detachment.
