That was overlooked when the brief was prepared, and I thought I should correct that at this point. I will not deal with all of the matters that Mr. Bourgon discussed in his submissions to you this morning. I will deal with the question that has been raised by the Chamber, question number 2. I will deal with the use of force and its impact on effective control. And I will deal with the question of de jure control. The either questions, I believe, are adequately addressed in our brief, and there's no need to respond further. Let me begin by answering the question. The question, as Mr. Bourgon properly pointed out, has two parts: First, identify the evidence pointing to Hadzihasanovic's failure to provide IHL training and to set up a disciplinary system to ensure compliance. And secondly, to respond as to whether such failure can itself attract criminal responsibility to Hadzihasanovic for failure to prevent the crimes of cruel treatment and the murder of Dragan Popovic. I, like Mr. Bourgon, will answer question -- part 2 of the question first. And our submission is directly contrary to his. Our submission is that on the facts of this case - and I stress that "on the facts of this case" - from the 13th of August, 1993, when the El Mujahedin Detachment became subordinated to Hadzihasanovic and the 3rd Corps, his failure to provide IHL training and to set up a disciplinary system to ensure compliance does itself attract criminal responsibility for failure to prevent the crimes of cruel treatment and the murder of Dragan Popovic. Why? First of all, reading from the judgement, paragraph 1479, "Hadzihasanovic knew the members of the El Mujahedin Detachment had a dangerous and violent temperament well before the detachment was integrated into the ABiH. In fact, he knew those troops had already committed heinous crimes, specifically the massacre of 24 Croats in Maline in June 1993 and the execution of four Croatian civilians in Miletici in April, in breach of IHL." In addition, the risk that he was aware of was exacerbated because the murders were never punished, because these crimes were not brought to the attention of the military police or military judicial authorities and unlikely to the civilian police and judiciary, given ongoing combat activities in the area. That's found in trial judgement paragraph 1433. The events that gave Hadzihasanovic knowledge of the risk of incorporating and subordinating this group to his 3rd Corps command are set out in paragraphs 1427 and 1435. And the Trial Chamber discussed whether Hadzihasanovic had reason to know of -- I'm sorry, let me back up for a second. These were -- these events are discussed and they became relevant for the discussion by the Trial Chamber as to what Hadzihasanovic had reason to know at the time of the October abductions. And during this discussion, the Trial Chamber also referred to the Totic abduction and the killing of his four bodyguards earlier in April. Now, although the Trial Chamber was aware of the Maline massacre and the killings in Miletici, he nevertheless recommended that the Mujahedin in his zone of responsibility be integrated into the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and re-subordinated to him as an independent unit with special status so he could use them immediately for combat. He was keenly aware of his accountability for their actions. In fact, he was concerned about being held accountable for their actions when they were not yet formally subordinated to him. And that's found in DH73 and trial judgement 552. Delic's response to Hadzihasanovic's concern on June the 13th about his accountability was responded to quickly by Commander Delic to the effect that: "Send these groups to Mount Igman and merge them with the SVK Independent Detachment in Zuka's unit. In case they do not accept, show them no hospitality and eventually disarm them." And that's found at paragraph 270 of -- or in the Exhibit P270. The same day Hadzihasanovic protested to Sefer Halilovic and asked that only the first part of the order be implemented. That's found in trial judgement 555. From this point forward, the 16th of June, 1993, Hadzihasanovic was part of the discussions and negotiations leading to the creation of the El Mujahedin Detachment and its subordination to the 3rd Corps. In spite of his concern for accountability, his knowledge of the risk of incorporating this group into the 3rd Corps, from the date of the re-subordination he took no steps to identify and isolate the perpetrators of the Miletici and Maline crimes and he took no steps to initiate criminal proceedings against the perpetrators of those crimes. He allowed the members of the El Mujahedin Detachment, including those responsible for the crimes, to remain isolated in their camps, to which the military police and security police had no access. Even access by commanders was tenuous, according to the trial judgement. And instead of taking even the most basic action, like training and establishing discipline, he rushed them to combat. He failed to address the risk of future crimes by the criminal members in the El Mujahedin Detachment. And on these facts, he can be held criminally responsible. The legal principles on which this submission is based are found in the trial judgement starting at paragraph 145 and continuing to paragraph 151. And the evidence showed that Hadzihasanovic did accept that the 3rd Corps must be subject to an internal disciplinary system, enforcing compliance with the rules of international humanitarian law and the law applicable to armed conflict, and that he, as the commander, was responsible for carrying out this task. And on this point, Mr. Bourgon and the Prosecution agreed. He also send his duty to disseminate those rules and to include them in the study in the programmes of military instruction. We agree there too. Hadzihasanovic, as commander of the 3rd Corps, by virtue of the authority vested in him, was qualified to exercise control over his troops and the weapons they use. More than anyone else, he could have prevented breaches by creating the appropriate frame of mind, ensuring rational use of means of combat, and by maintaining discipline. And he was aware, based on his concerns as early as June 13th, 1993, that criminal liability could attach for his failure to meet his duty as commander in respect of his newly-formed El Mujahedin Detachment. As commander of the 3rd Corps, he had choices. He could either take measures to instil order and discipline, or not. In respect of the newly-formed El Mujahedin Detachment, he chose not to take measures. Aware of the risk presented by members of the newly-subordinated El Mujahedin Detachment, Hadzihasanovic took the risk that his failures to take even the most basic measures to prevent crimes by them while under his command and the risk resulted in this conviction from which he's appealed to you today. While failure to take basic measures did not -- does not necessarily result in criminal liability, on the facts of this case it did. The Trial Chamber appreciated that failure to take general measures may lead to criminal responsibility. It stated, and I believe this is paragraph 161 [sic]: "Those general measures will, however, be taken into consideration in the factual analysis and evaluation of efforts made by the accused to fulfil their obligation to prevent, in view of the circumstances of the case. In fact, it is much less foreseeable for violations of international humanitarian law to occur when a commander has taken a series of general preventative measures to instil order and discipline in his troops than when a commander has not taken care to put in place a system which instills respect for the law and discipline." This statement is consistent with the recent Appeals Chamber decision in Halilovic at paragraphs 63 and 64. "What constitutes" - and I'm quoting - "What constitutes necessary and reasonable measures to fulfil a commander's duty is not a matter of substantive law but of evidence." And continuing: "The correct legal standard is solely whether the superior failed to take the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent the criminal act or punish the perpetrator thereof. Of course, the single standard will have to be applied differently in different circumstances." Our position simply is that the Appeal Chamber's single standard applied to Halilovic's failure to provide basic training and to set up a disciplinary system for the El Mujahedin, in light of the knowledge that he had of their past criminal conduct, and to ensure their compliance with it, the disciplinary system and the rules that they would be taught, does by itself on the special and unique circumstances of this case attract criminal liability, as the Trial Chamber found. And therefore, he was properly found to be guilty of failure to take necessary and reasonable measures to prevent the crimes of cruel treatment and the murder of Dragan Popovic on this basis. This takes me to part 1 of the question. And this question flows from the Trial Chamber's conclusions at paragraphs 1479 to 1484. These conclusions were informed by what Hadzihasanovic knew about the El Mujahedin before he recommended and accepted their integration into the 3rd Corps and subordination as an independent detachment of the 3rd Corps. On August 13th, 1993, when Hadzihasanovic received the order re-subordinating the El Mujahedin Detachment to the 3rd Corps, he knew it included murderers of Croatian citizens and Croatian POWs in violation of IHL. Given that in Hadzihasanovic's zone of responsibility the fighting was against Croatian forces and for the territory -- for a territory with Croatian residents, this knowledge alone, in combination with his knowledge of their past crimes, required Hadzihasanovic to implement measures to prevent the commission of similar crimes by his newly-subordinated members while they remained under his command. Instead, Hadzihasanovic put military necessity over international humanitarian law principles. He accepted their independent and special status so that they could be used in combat. He permitted them to maintain their two isolated camps near Mehurici, the Poljanice camp and the Orasac camp, separate from the 3rd Corps and the OG BK main troops. The location of the camps and separation made policing breaches of discipline more difficult, because access and communication were precarious. Reference trial judgement 833, 849, and 1405. While the El Mujahedin recruits were being trained for 40 days at these camps, the El Mujahedin were not part of the training offered by the ABiH in the area. That's paragraph 598. Hadzihasanovic accepted the order re-subordinating the El Mujahedin Detachment and with three -- within three days acted to re-subordinate them to the OG BK for immediate use in combat. And that is Exhibit P671. In spite of his knowledge of -- of the past violent and dangerous -- dangerous temperament of some of the members of the El Mujahedin Detachment, he did not include in his orders to the commander of the OG BK any notice about the criminal propensity of the members he was re-subordinating them to or proposing to, or instructions on measures to prevent the commission of the crimes by them. The Trial Chamber was correct to consider Hadzihasanovic's actions in the context of Hadzihasanovic's steps before August 13th to make the ABiH a more professional and disciplined army. The steps included - and Mr. Bourgon has referred to it, and I'll just summarise it - orders on training soldiers in IHL, orders on ensuring military discipline prevailed. The military discipline orders demanded more military police resources and reminded the military police of their obligations.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you for slowing down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Reminded the military police of their obligations within the framework the Presidency has legislated. Paragraphs 859 and 872. The Trial Chamber's conclusion that no IHL training and military discipline system was created for the El Mujahedin Detachment is summarised as 1434. Its analysis proceeds from the finding that the El Mujahedin Detachment was integrated into the ABiH on August 13th, 1993. Before this date, the Trial Chamber found that the El Mujahedin Detachment was not integrated in the ABiH and therefore could not have benefitted from the measures that Hadzihasanovic, as 3rd Corps commander, had instructed and ordered for his nearly 30.000 troops under his command. What was done before 13 August is detailed in paragraphs 1161 to 1167, under the heading "General Measures," and in 856 to 859 as to training. Hadzihasanovic attempted to stress the importance of training the troops, especially new recruits. He drew attention to IHL principles and organised distribution of Geneva Conventions. Hadzihasanovic emphasised the obligation to subordinates. He created a legal department to instruct officers in legal obligations assigned to brigades during armed combat. He issued orders prohibiting the detention of civilians and mistreatment of POWs on pain of sanctions. He asked for investigations into reports on alleged unlawful detentions and mistreatments, sometimes reports to him personally. In sum, Hadzihasanovic had the power to issue orders for training and discipline and to have them enforced. Of course, as commander of the 3rd Corps, he had power over all aspects of the 3rd Corps as well, including issuing combat orders, re-subordination orders, allocating resources and equipment, et cetera. In contrast to these previous positive measures to create and enforce a functioning military discipline system that were taken before the 13th of August, 1993, the system for some reason did not apply and Hadzihasanovic did not make it apply to the El Mujahedin Detachment. He ordered no -- he ordered no such measures for that detachment after their re-subordination to and integration into the corps. The Trial Chamber's finding at 1434 of a lack of training and an absence of a military disciplinary system for the members of the El Mujahedin Detachment after 13 August found further support in Hadzihasanovic's rush to assign them to combat. The Trial Chamber discussed this at paragraphs 18 -- 812, I'm sorry, to 830. I'll just summarise what those paragraphs say. On August 12th, Hadzihasanovic stressed the urgent need to organise and make use of foreign volunteers. As early as August 16th, Hadzihasanovic sent a letter to the commander of the OG BK advising that 50 members of the El Mujahedin Detachment were ready to go to the front at Zavidovici and sought a reply the next day. Then on August 28th he ordered the El Mujahedin re-subordinated to the 306th Brigade. Its special status allowed it to refuse the order. The El Mujahedin Detachment was officially re-subordinated to the OG BK on September 6th, owing to imminent combat operations. From this date, the El Mujahedin Detachment participated in continuous combat as part of the OG BK until October 31st, when Hadzihasanovic left his post as commander of the 3rd Corps. The Trial Chamber noted that the September 6th re-subordination order did not instruct or direct any training or solving of the problems that were known to exist in the El Mujahedin Detachment and it contrasted the order of September 6th with an order of December 4th, 1993, re-subordinating the El Mujahedin to the OG BK, where greater clarity, in terms of the measures to be taken in respect of their re-subordination, were discussed. The Trial Chamber at paragraph 1482 highlights that Hadzihasanovic did not have to use untrained men in combat and concludes that he should not have used them. And I -- and they're talking there about the use of the El Mujahedin in combat prior to undergoing proper training and being part of a discipline system. Quoting from paragraph 1482: "Furthermore, he accepted the special status of the El Mujahedin Detachment as soon as it began working with the ABiH by deciding to derive military benefit from the El Mujahedin Detachment in those conditions, despite the alarming information at his disposal, Hadzihasanovic must have foreseen, well before the Croatian civilians were abducted in October 1993, the potential consequences of that abduction." In conclusion, there was ample evidence to support the Trial Chamber's conclusion on the facts of this case that Hadzihasanovic's failure to provide IHL training and to set up a disciplinary system for the newly-recruited El Mujahedin Detachment attracted criminal responsibility that resulted from his failure -- in his being convicted for failure to prevent the crimes of cruel treatment and the murder of Dragan Popovic in October of 1993. I'll now move on to the use-of-force argument. The appropriate measures to be taken by a commander are gauged by considering the power of the superior. And the trial judgement gets this correct, I would submit, at paragraph 170. In his argument, Hadzihasanovic argues that his failure to exercise his power to prevent his subordinates from committing or continuing to commit crimes equates to lack of effective control and lack of material ability to prevent or punish. But I would -- the Prosecution would submit that his argument confuses his power as commander of the 3rd Corps with his will to use this power. His position as commander of the 3rd Corps vested in him the power and the authority to control the troops subordinated to him. He demonstrated his power and authority in issuing orders and instructions and in having them enforced. His argument on this point accepts that he, as commander, possessed the power and therefore the means to prevent by use of force, but suggests that the -- having to resort to force to prevent crimes negates his effective control. Contrary to his argument, the object and purpose of the doctrine of command responsibility and the theory of responsible command support the use of force to prevent a crime when necessary, if exercised in a reasonable manner. Resort to force against subordinates committing or about to commit is a reasonable and necessary measure consistent with the commander's responsibility to prevent crimes by his subordinates. Whether it is instructing officers to stop the commission of crimes on pain of being forcibly arrested, on -- on pain of being detained, and if they resist the arrest, on pain of perhaps being shot, if it's an armed resistance. Hadzihasanovic argues that when a commander concludes that resort to force is required to prevent a crime, his duty to prevent is suspended and he is freed from any potential criminal responsibility for failing to prevent his subordinates from committing the crime or being about to commit the crime. The Trial Chamber appreciated that a commander with only limited number of soldiers and materials may find it difficult to use force against his own troops who have breached IHL. As a result, they concluded that he may be determined not to have the material ability to prevent or punish for violations of IHL. But they found clearly - and I think it's obvious, given his status as commander of the 3rd Corps with 30.000 soldiers at his disposal - that Hadzihasanovic had no such limitation. In fact, Hadzihasanovic had at his disposal a police force, a military police force of 400 to 450 members specifically attached to the 3rd Corps command. The 3rd Corps had substantial weaponry at its disposal. He didn't lack the -- the power to take appropriate measures the prevent the Orasac crimes; he lacked the will to act. His unwillingness to act triggers his criminal responsibility. It does not excuse it. Finally, the Trial Chamber correctly held that a commander who uses soldiers while knowing there is a serious risk that they will not obey his orders to comply with IHL may not claim to have lacked effective control over them to avoid responsibility under Article 7(3). They found - and we support this, the position that led to this finding - that his conduct before the crimes is relevant to establish that he accepted the risk that the troops may not follow his orders. And this takes us back to the extensive discussion of the Trial Chamber, and a very discerning one, that there were many, many, many pieces of evidence that indicated de facto control of the Mujahedin by the 3rd Corps command, but there were -- there was other evidence that raised a reasonable doubt. But they were entitled to look at all of that evidence in the context of what happened from June through to August, preceding the August 13th re-subordination order and subsequent, to conclude that Hadzihasanovic accepted the risk. He in fact encouraged the re-subordination with full knowledge of what they had done or what some of the members had done. And on the basis of his acceptance, it can't be said that -- to hide behind his acceptance and say, But things went terribly wrong and therefore I had no effective control, particularly when he never made any efforts during the course of the time that he was commander of the 3rd Corps, to ensure that this unit was properly controlled when it became integrated into the 3rd Corps. I now propose to move to the final point. And I've touched on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Kremer. Judge Meron would like to ask something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Kremer, this question that you have now been discussing of the obligation to use force or the capacity to use force is a very hard one, in my view, and I would like to explore it with you further. We heard your argument about it. We heard Mr. -- We heard Mr. Bourgon's argument. His argument was that Mr. Hadzihasanovic, as you -- you have heard, lacked both de jure and de facto effective control. He argued that the acknowledgment by the Trial Court, the trial judgement, that force would have to be used to establish control indicated that whatever the de jure situation, effective control was lacking. Now, I don't want to speak to the question of training. I just want to focus on this question on -- on -- of the use of force. It seems to me that both you and Mr. Bourgon are agreed about the criterion to be applied. And the criterion is a military commander would have to take the necessary and the reasonable measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: So let's proceed on that basis. So here you yourself spoke several times about the circumstances of this case. So the approach has to be sort of contextual. So here are a few questions that come to mind that I would be very grateful if you would enlighten me on that, and I'm sure that my colleagues from the Bench would benefit. How large was the Mujahedin contingent in the two camps that you have mentioned? What casualties would be -- would have the force loyal to Mr. Hadzihasanovic have to take to establish control? How likely was success? And how would then an attack on the Mujahedin forces affect the overall campaign for Mr. -- which Mr. Hadzihasanovic was responsible of -- of conducting a war? On a more abstract level, Mr. Kremer, how likely does it have to be that any given measure would be successful before such a measure could be considered necessary and reasonable? I think I gave you enough questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Okay. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: May I, in this context, before you answer, add a question of a general nature maybe on this same point, and ask you how much - it's related to the question - how much you feel there should be in this -- in the use of force a proportionality test.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon [sic], just to continue the President's question, which I think is excellent, imagine that the force that -- that the Mujahedin consist of five or ten Mujahedin. The argument for using force would be, I think, overwhelming. Where does it -- where -- at which point -- where is the -- the sort of threshold or parameters where this thing becomes complicated, in terms of proportionality?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: The issue rests with the commander that is confronted with the situation of troops who are committing crimes. He has the duty to prevent the commission of the crimes, and he has to make an assessment based on what he knows as to what to do, because he is required by law to take the necessary measures to prevent the crime and to take reasonable measures to prevent the crime. The problem that you've asked are -- or the -- the questions, the first five questions, go to the question of reasonableness, as opposed to necessary measures. I remind the Appeals Chamber that the discussion by the Trial Chamber on this question rested with the fact that nothing was done other than the passive negotiation with the Mujahedin in the unit who had seized the Croatian civilians and that previous threats of violence, mortar shelling their camp, pointing an artillery implement at their camp, had led to more positive results than occurred in this particular case. And the issue for Hadzihasanovic, which the Trial Chamber discussed at considerable length, was what, if anything, should I do and what can I do? They concluded that he could not launch an attack, because he didn't have the time. He had the means to launch an attack, should that have been necessary, but it was never determined to have been necessary. He -- he certainly had the means. The assessment of reasonable and necessary would have to take account, as Judge Meron properly points out, all of the relevant factors for determining whether or not to take -- or what means to take, and are they reasonable and necessary, including how large was the Mujahedin contingent in the camp. Mr. Bourgon can correct me if I'm wrong, but my understanding was, based on the evidence, that there were about 100 to 150 Mujahedin in the two camps in total, but at the time we should also remember that many of them would have been in combat, outside of the area. There is evidence by witnesses to the effect that at the time that Alagic and his assistant went to the Orasac camp in order to start negotiations, they saw there a number of armed men but several unarmed. They saw, I think - and I had the evidence here, but I'll just go from memory - approximately three armed men and ten unarmed men. The -- there is evidence on the record from -- in the Poljanice camp that on one of the visits by one of the witnesses there was one armed guard at the entrance to the camp. The question is: How large was the contingent? It could have been as large as 100 to 150. Was it that large? We would submit probably not. But it was up to Hadzihasanovic to inform himself of that information and make the appropriate assessment. What casualties would have resulted as a result of an armed attack? The question [sic] is it depends on the resources of the two forces. Whether the show of force, as the Trial Chamber, we would submit, properly concluded, may have been sufficient to end the hostage-taking there and then. But we don't know what the result would have been, because nothing was done or very little was done. What casual -- whether there would have been civilian casualties, I think the evidence is that Mehurici was basically the -- an IKM and it was basically military. There would not have been in those camps at the -- at the very least, any collateral damage of -- to civilians or civilian property. How likely was it -- would it have been of success? It would depend -- it would depend on the measure that was taken, whether it was -- the Trial Chamber concluded that the -- the display or the -- the display of force -- the intention to use force or, at least, mounting the resources in order to use force, accompanying with a threat, may have been successful. That's where they say he failed to act reasonably and necessarily. They didn't say that using force against this group was the only measure that he could take. In fact, they said there -- there were a number of reasonable necessary measures that might have been successful. And what it escalates to, and if it escalates there, depends on the circumstances. The -- the Trial Chamber, by my reading of the judgement, does not say that that was the only measure and that was the only reasonable measure. Far from it. And I think, with respect to Mr. Bourgon's submission, he takes the extreme example and attempts to weave it into a legal principle, and it just -- it doesn't work. I think I've answered the question of proportionality. Proportionality depends on the circumstances as they continue along the -- the period of time, and it's based on the information that the commander has and is continuing to obtain, that will inform his decisions and will inform the -- the actions that he takes against the non -- the criminals who are about to commit crimes or are in the process of committing crimes. If there's a crime that's being committed, if -- if they know that they are going to be murdered, then he would have to make an assessment. In terms of my obligation to prevent these murders, what should I do? Should I use force? How much force? And the use of force would be chosen, having a regard to the risk. And so it's a risk/reward, as in any hostage-taking, the facts are going to vary on a case-by-case basis. On this case, we have the simple fact that not even a -- a more serious threat was issued when the second group of hostages were taken. That is what, I think, underlies the Trial Chamber's decision that Hadzihasanovic is guilty for having to fail -- having failed to prevent the crimes in Orasac. Just on the de jure argument, the Trial Chamber's decision is, in our submission, a very discerning one. They spent several hundred paragraphs dealing with the question of de facto control prior to August 13th. And as I've previously alluded to, there was substantial discussion on measures that would point to de facto control and measures that did not. And ultimately, the conclusion of the Trial Chamber was that the evidence did not, beyond a reasonable doubt, establish effective control. And they very -- I'm sorry. They very carefully analysed the events leading to the August 13th subordination order by Rasim Delic, which included, as I've already mentioned on a couple of occasions, the involvement and recommendation of Hadzihasanovic. The fact that the group, the El Mujahedin Detachment, was -- was subordinated is supported by a lot of evidence before and after August 13th. We've outlined much of it in our appeal brief -- or our response brief to Mr. Bourgon's submissions. But there is additional evidence. During August of 1993, there was a -- there's evidence on the record to the effect that soldiers from other units, as a result of a call put out by the Mujahedin that they were conducting a training programme, started to leave in order to be trained by them and to join the El Mujahedin Detachment. And there was much made of this at -- at trial, that that was having the effect of weakening some of the units because of the departures. But what that shows, in combination with the move to create an El Mujahedin Detachment, is that the -- the interested parties were starting to assemble at Mehurici for the official order, and in fact no Mujahedin were joining in combat with the 3rd Corps during this period and there was anticipation of the proposed order to create an independent detachment. So the -- the evidence clearly shows that there is ample support for the conclusion that on the 13th of August the de jure order was made and the de jure order was made with the consent of the people who were -- the -- the focus of it, and it was made with the -- the consent and affirmation of the commander, who would benefit from additional combat troops after that date, combat troops which he proved he could subordinate and proved he could command. The fact that he chose not to implement the appropriate measures to prevent them from committing crimes and to prevent them from -- and to punish them, should he want, was his personal choice because of his willingness or desire to use them immediately in combat but also because at that point military necessity overtook his obligations, or what he believed his obligations were as a military commander. Our position is he was properly found to be de jure commander at that time. The proof of effective control as a result of the de jure command was carefully analysed as well. The Trial Chamber looked at several pieces of communication between Hadzihasanovic and others showing that the El Mujahedin Detachment was referred to in the order itself, something that was not common previous to August 13th. They spoke of and found that there was -- it was clear that Hadzihasanovic had the final say over where the unit would go. There's communication that's referred to in the judgement between the commander of OG Istok and Hadzihasanovic about -- about the issue. There are reports in the war diaries referring to El Mujahedin losses, which wasn't the case prior to August 13th. There are many, many indicators that the El Mujahedin Detachment became incorporated. Were they a problem? Yes. Were they -- were they not his subordinates? The answer is "no." Did Hadzihasanovic have effective control over them to the extent that he had the material ability to prevent and punish? The answer is "yes." He was a commander of a 30.000-man army with military police at his disposal and the authority to issue commands to all those under him in a combat situation where orders mattered. He knew that at the time he accepted them into his unit, he did nothing to ensure that they would abide by his orders, and the consequences resulted in the cruel treatment of the Croatian civilians in October and their -- the death of Dragan Popovic. Subject to any questions that you may have, the remainder of my response to Mr. Bourgon's submissions is found in our response brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRACOL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honours, I'm now going to respond to the fourth ground of appeal of Hadzihasanovic, related to the Zenica music school. Hadzihasanovic has challenged the findings of the Trial Chamber according to which he had reason to know of the serious physical abuse committed by subordinates in the Zenica music school. And secondly, that Hadzihasanovic failed to take all the reasonable and necessary measures to prevent and punish his subordinates. Your Honours, Hadzihasanovic has failed to show any error in the judgement. The Prosecution relies on its response brief, which fully supports our request to dismiss the fourth ground of appeal submitted by Hadzihasanovic. With respect to the disposition of the judgement referred to by Mr. Bourgon, we would like to refer you to paragraphs 179 and 180 of our appeals brief. I have nothing to add to that. But I would just like to respond to the submissions of Hadzihasanovic related to the attempts of his subordinates to conceal the serious physical abuse meted out to his -- to victims at the Zenica music school. This fact, the fact that he tried to conceal the fact, is irrelevant and it has no impact on his criminal liability. Mr. Bourgon dedicated the bulk of his submissions to this attempt, but his submissions are irrelevant because they ignore the fact that the Trial Chamber correctly found that Hadzihasanovic had reason to know, since the 8th of May, 1993, that his subordinates had committed serious physical abuse at the Zenica music school but he took no action, because sources outside the 7th Brigade, such as the ECMM, the HVO, and Judge Vlado Adamovic, a witness who was an investigating judge at the Zenica district military court in 1993 and 1994, had provided him with, and I quote "alarming information that his subordinates were committing mistreatment." I would like to refer you to paragraphs 1230 and 1236 of the trial judgement. The Prosecution has tendered a lot of evidence about Hadzihasanovic's knowledge at trial, and I would like to outline two of these examples that you will find at page 224 of its final trial brief. First of all, Judge Adamovic testified about a meeting attended by Hadzihasanovic and the ECMM, a meeting that was cochaired by Ambassador Jean-Pierre Thebault of the ECMM, his deputy, and the president of the Zenica military district court. The meeting took place at the Hotel Internacional in Zenica. During the meeting, Judge Adamovic stated that he raised the mistreatment at the music school. Hadzihasanovic told him that he himself had heard of people being beaten up with wooden bats; therefore, Hadzihasanovic admitted knowledge. And I would like to refer you to transcript 9482 to 9483 of 24th June 2004. The Trial Chamber duly considered Judge Adamovic's warnings to Hadzihasanovic, warnings referring to physical abuse suffered by prisoners. At paragraph 1221 of the judgement. A second example of evidence: On the 7th of May, 1993, Hadzihasanovic was informed by a letter sent to him by Tihomir Blaskic, who was complaining, and I quote, "of extreme mistreatments of detainees," and I'd like to quote the document in English: [In English] "People brought to the KP Dom from the music school have been beaten up and are in a very bad state." [Interpretation] And this is Exhibit P3593. As a result, Hadzihasanovic was made aware of these serious mistreatments on the 8th of May, 1993. Once again, the Trial Chamber duly considered the specific information provided to Hadzihasanovic at paragraph 1208 of the judgement. Under these circumstances, the Trial Chamber duly and rightly decided to ignore the testimony of HF, according to which Nesib Talic, who was the 7th Brigade assistant commander in charge of military security, was misusing the stamp of the 7th Brigade and was always concealing things to Hadzihasanovic. The findings of the Trial Chamber are therefore reasonable. Contrary to Mr. Bourgon's submission this morning, the Trial Chamber has not decided to ignore the testimony of Dzemal Merdan, who was the 3rd Corps deputy commander, and of Witness HF, who was also a senior officer of the 3rd Corps command. On the contrary, the Trial Chamber has duly examined and considered these statements and they questioned the exactitude of these statements. First of all, Dzemal Merdan and HF failed to mention any specific dates for their visits. I would like to refer you to Dzemal Merdan's testimony on the 16th of December, 2004, transcript page 13632. The Trial Judges referred to these transcripts in footnote 2694 of the judgement and Hadzihasanovic also referred to this in -- in his -- in footnote 324 of his appeal brief. The Trial Chamber referred to the testimony of Witness HF, page 17214 and 17215 of the transcript. The Trial Judges have duly considered this testimony and have made no error in their assessment. Secondly, the Trial Chamber questioned the exactitude of the statements of Dzemal Merdan and HF, since these visits could not have been concentrated between 11th and 15th of June, 1993. For this, they relied on the statements of Dzemal Merdan and HF. This demonstrates that the Trial Judges carefully analysed and considered the testimonies of these witnesses in-depth and it also shows that the Trial Chamber Judges provided a reasoned opinion for their findings. The Trial Chamber's reasons are not unreasonable because they gave more weight to evidence from other witnesses about mistreatments. Paragraph 1238 of the judgement. The Trial Judges assessed the testimony of Dzemal Merdan and Witness HF against the testimony of many former detainees held at the music school in Zenica between 18th of April, 1993 and 20th of August, 1993. For example, at paragraph 1190 of the judgement. Their findings are therefore reasonable, in light of a lack of specificity of Witnesses Dzemal Merdan and HF. In conclusion, Your Honours, first of all, there is no dispute that serious physical abuse was committed against Bosnian Croats and Bosnian Serbs and prisoners of war held at the Zenica music school. Hadzihasanovic has admitted this, for example, at paragraph 110(a) of his reply brief. Secondly, there is no issue that Hadzihasanovic's subordinates committed such serious physical abuse. Thirdly, Hadzihasanovic had reason to know of the serious physical abuse, since he received, and I quote, "alarming information pertaining to this on the 8th of May, 1993." Fourthly, and lastly, the Trial Chamber correctly found that Hadzihasanovic, as a commander, failed to take the necessary and reasonable measures commensurate with the situation. He did not make genuine efforts to initiate an appropriate investigation into the allegations of cruel treatments. These are the findings of the Trial Chamber at paragraph 1240 of the judgement. That is the reason why the Trial Chamber did not make any error in convicting Hadzihasanovic for his failure to take all the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent and punish crimes committed by his subordinates in the Zenica music school. The Prosecution requests that Your Honours dismiss the fourth ground of appeal raised by Hadzihasanovic. Of course, I am available for any questions you may have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There seems to me no questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRACOL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, so these are our submissions, our final submissions to the appeal raised by Mr. Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. We're going to break now for 20 minutes. Thereafter, we shall have the reply by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I will now give the floor to the Defence of Mr. Hadzihasanovic for the reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I will address the issues which we feel have a more important bearing on the adjudication of this appeal. I will start with the arguments which were raised in response by the Prosecution concerning the events in Bugojno. First of all, in light of the corrections which were brought to the transcript, it is our submission that the Trial Chamber's conclusions where it held that "seems to indicate" about Witness Muratovic is incorrect. Moreover, the language in the corrected translations of the original audio transcript make it clear, in light of the context mentioned earlier, that a criminal report had been filed and measures taken in accordance with the law. Concerning the arguments raised about Witness Zeric that he did not receive a criminal report, one, this is not a most important issue; two, what this witness said when he testified is that he divided all the reports he received. He only was responsible for part of the reports which were sent to the Travnik district military prosecutor, and he also said in response in cross-examination that he did not verify the record before testifying and that he would have to do so in order to determine whether in fact there was a report filed or not. Regarding the jurisdiction of the municipal prosecutor, contrary to the arguments of the Prosecution, the Bugojno municipal prosecutor could have jurisdiction and that would happen if the offence was committed jointly by civilians and soldiers together. The evidence reveals that we know about the involvement of two soldiers and the evidence also reveals that more perpetrators were involved. Were these civilians? We don't know. But he could have jurisdiction and he could exercise it. Whether himself, if it was a crime, anything below murder. And if it was murder, he would have to transfer it to the Zenica high public prosecutor and the Zenica high court. But in any event, what the Prosecution said today is significant. What my colleague said is that he was not -- he had not -- did not have jurisdiction and in such a case he would have to refer the matter to the district military court. But we agree, if he did not have jurisdiction, it was his duty to transfer the case to the district military prosecutor. But what bearing does this have on this case is that the military took action. They put the people in gaol. They put the criminal report. And now the military prosecutor has the matter and it's his responsibility to transfer it. The military is aware and the duty of the commander at all levels has been fulfilled to take necessary and reasonable measures. Regarding the mens rea for after 18 August, the standard to be applied is that developed by the Appeals Chamber in Celebici. We say the Trial Chamber in this case departed from this standard. If we follow the proper application of this standard in Krnojelac, also by the Appeals Chamber, the careful analysis that was then performed by the Appeals Chamber, who concluded that Krnojelac had alarming information, well, in this case if we perform the same type of analysis and we look at the Trial Chamber's findings, then we easily come to the conclusion that General Hadzihasanovic did not have reason to know that his soldiers would commit any similar criminal crimes after 18 August. One important fact is important in this regard, is that in this case, there was a measure taken by General Hadzihasanovic. There was a measure taken from the 307 Brigade. The people were put in gaol. And that is important when we put this into the equation and the analysis to be performed, as the Appeals Chamber did in Krnojelac. I recently attended a ICRC expert meeting on sanctions. A report is about to come out pretty soon. The conclusions of that expert group said - and of course, it's not binding law, but that's what they -- that's what the experts were saying then - the best sanction to ensure the application of international humanitarian law, it must be immediate, it must be visible, and it must be close to the situation where the offence happened. In this case, everything that was done in this case fulfils that definition and those requirements. The soldiers are in prison and a criminal report has been filed. I don't see how can this be an encouragement to do more deeds of the same type to anyone. Moving on to the Mujahedin. First of all, I'd like to point out for the record that it appears to me, from hearing my colleague, that he cited many conclusions and many -- a lot of wording from the judgement, but he did not cite the evidence that goes with it. It is when you look at this evidence that you find that numerous conclusions of fact and the numerous inferences drawn by the Trial Chamber that were simply incorrect and that could not be drawn by a reasonable trier of fact. On the training issue, the prior notice developed -- a theory developed by my colleague is simply incorrect. If I listen to him, it means that General Hadzihasanovic was responsible for anything that the Mujahedin would do after 13 August 1993, because he did not train them. The thing is there's a reason why and if they were not trained. It's that it was not possible. According to the evidence, these people would not even receive a phone call. According to the evidence, they would not let access to their camps. According to the evidence, they didn't -- the 3rd Corps did not even know where one of the camps was, and that is the Orasac camp. And it also ignores the issue that we have to also look at the crime that was supposed to be prevented by this training. The theory of the Prosecution simply doesn't hold ground. On page 18, my colleague said that all what the General did concerning training and setting up a disciplinary system -- and he was very, for the first time I was glad to hear the Prosecution commenting so highly on General Hadzihasanovic, because this is what the evidence on the record reveals, a top-level commander who took measures at all times. If he didn't do it, it's because it was not possible. Then again, my colleague has avoided the question that there's no evidence on the record specifically answering the question posed by the Trial Chamber that he did not train the Mujahedin and that he did not put in place a disciplinary system. The most important part comes with the use of force. The use of force; we believe that the Prosecution's theory, once again, is entirely incorrect. Responsible command imposes obligations on the commander for his subordinates. That's the basis of the complete responsible command theory. A commander, he has subordinates and in respect of these subordinates, he must train them, he must order them to apply the law, and if they don't, then he has obligation towards them. The -- the basic principle is subordination. This is why, according to Article 7(3) of the Statute, we have existence of a superior-to-subordinate relationship. And this relationship, according to the case-law of the Tribunal, is fulfilled by showing effective control. And the question here is very simple: Does effective control, as been defined as the material ability to prevent or punish? And according to the case-law of the International Tribunal, the use of force is not included in this -- in the material ability to prevent or punish. In the end, this shows that these Mujahedin, those rogue elements who were present - it was not denied; they were there - but they were never subordinates of General Hadzihasanovic. Let's say we take the position that was argued with the Prosecution with the fact that it -- use of force is included in material ability. Then we say that if material ability in such a case includes authority under domestic law, a commander can not just attack his subordinates without any authority under domestic law. It is not the same. Attacking the enemy is war; attacking your own is using force against your own -- in your own army. You can't do that unless you have domestic authority and the proper military authority. Let's say, again, because this was discussed in the presentation of my colleague, that it is the case that it can be -- it is possible to use force and then the -- the question becomes whether the use of force was reasonable and necessary in the circumstances. In response to the questions which were posed by the Judges, how large was the force to be attacked? We don't know from the evidence. We can assume a whole bunch of things from what my colleague said. It cannot be -- it cannot be established on the basis of the evidence how much force were present, starting in 20 August 1993 -- or 20 October 1993 in Orasac. Worse, they didn't even know where Orasac was. They didn't even know that Orasac was a camp. How could they attack a location that they don't even know exists? The chances of success, the Trial Chamber concluded, were reasonable, or something like that. This is entirely contrary to what the military expert said. We've had some pretty high-level military officers testify in this case. General Karavelic is the officer who defended Sarajevo against the worst possible blockade in years. This guy came and he shared his knowledge and he also shared his own experience when he had to attack former subordinates, subordinates who were suddenly became out of control. They were part of his army before, but they were completely out of control. He went to see the president of Bosnia and he said, Let me -- I need to attack these people, but I'm not going to do it unless I get the proper authority, and the president said, Yes. He gave them the authority after doing the proper political analysis. The time required to plan such an operation was not addressed in the judgement. In terms of the impact on the overall campaign, it was not assessed in the evidence, whether it was possible to launch such an attack at that time; whether there was enough soldiers. My colleague says, oh, yes, he's commanding a force of 30.000 soldiers. It's impossible, he has everything he can do. That's not what the evidence reveals, Mr. President. The evidence reveals that they were short of soldiers. Any one soldier employed to launch an attack on the Mujahedin in October of 1993 would be sacrificing a part of his mission. And that is -- was not addressed in terms of whether that was good or that was possible or not. It's not in the evidence. I could say it was and I really believe that it was, but who am I to say? What matters is the evidence in this case. The number of casualties that would result from such an attack, not assessed in the case. No evidence on this. Proportionality, no evidence on this. Proportionality is an obligation. If General Hadzihasanovic was about to launch an attack in Orasac -- or first he would like -- he would have to know where it is and that -- who is there and what's happening there and how it's defended and what weapons are used. Then he would have to you -- to evaluate proportionality and he could not evaluate proportionality. I'm told I have five minutes. I will make it quick.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, before you move to that point, are you moving to another issue. Are you going to move to another issue or remaining on this issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm moving to another issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: So perhaps before you go to that issue, how would you take the -- what would be your position if instead of putting the question that you put of the authority to use force, in terms of domestic law? You would have to deal with that in terms of international law, because assessing command responsibility is not a matter for domestic law. It is a matter for international law. And what, if you were asked to see whether the use of force, the authority had to be found in international law? How would you take the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I respectfully disagree with your position. I don't think international law would have to be assessed in such a case, because now we are looking at whether he has the -- he -- it was reasonable and necessary and where -- whether he has the material ability, and the material ability is based on a national standard, not an international standard. Whether a commander can use force against his subordinates is different from whether he can use force against the enemy in an armed conflict. It's two different concepts. The second one is entirely international. The first one, against your own subordinates, we submit, that you need this domestic authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I move on. Maybe I'd like to address one thing which I -- on this issue which my colleague raised. He said it was a lack of will to attack the Mujahedin, that he did not want. Well, first of all, we say that the evidence does not reveal that there was any lack of will to attack and that that is not -- that does not stem from the evidence. But whether he decides to attack, he may decide to attack. There might be a need for him to attack, but not in any relationship to his responsibility towards his subordinates. If he decides to attack, it's because the presence of these uncontrolled rogue elements is an impediment to his mission, and then he says, To accomplish my mission, I've got to get rid of these people and I will attack them. That's completely different. But it also shows, once again, if he wants to get rid of some people, it's because they are uncontrollable and not under the command and control of the 3rd Corps. About the de jure order, very quickly. The Delic order. When the Appeals Chamber will look at the evidence, it will see that there's no formal follow-up to the Delic order, no stamps of approval. All the procedure to enter a unit in the organisations were not followed. That's what I was referring to when I mentioned Witness Poparic. There was no order. And the order itself stated not 13 August as a date. It started, We said that you start taking measures to enter them into the organisation. And there was no agreement, and that video that my colleague refers to simply is not reliable evidence and there was never any agreement on the record where we can say there's an agreement between the army and the Mujahedin. I finish on music school very quickly. Simply by saying that what my -- the argument raised by my colleague, with all due respect, is circular and is not helpful in these circumstances. He said General Hadzihasanovic had knowledge. Yeah, we say that. We agree. We agree that some information was brought to the attention of General Hadzihasanovic of potential mistreatment in the music school. The issue is: What did he do? He sent his most senior officers. They go and they find nothing. They testify and the Chamber doesn't believe them. That's the issue. Why did the Chamber -- Trial Chamber not believe the highest senior officer he can send? That's the best he can do in the circumstances. They come back and they are not there. Why? Because there is concealment. And the efforts to conceal this information is on the record. The record shows that there was an effort. They were taken by bus to one of the close brigades -- a brigade that was close by. The Trial Chamber's analysis as to when did this take place is certainly not sufficient to disregard. My colleague -- I'd like simply to say something about my colleague raised an issue about Adamovic and about a meeting. The evidence reveals that the date of this meeting is not sure. He doesn't know when this meeting took place and if it was the meeting described by my colleague. That's very important. Finally, I just have one quick correction to make to something I said during my main submission, and that was on page 7, line 8. I needed to say I made a mistake concerning Exhibit DH337, it was Article 48 and also at trial transcript page 36, lines 13 to 17. I mentioned the documents which were used by the Trial Chamber in determining whether there was de jure control. My colleague referred to these documents, but he forgot to refer to the fact that there's only six of them. And what I'm telling -- saying today is that out of these six documents, only one was signed by General Hadzihasanovic; the others were not signed by him, and there -- there is testimony, including that of Kulenovic, to explain these documents on the record. This concludes my submissions in response to the grounds -- to the arguments raised by the Prosecution in response, and I would be glad to answer any questions you may have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I believe we have no questions. This concludes, then, the submissions of the parties in this appeal. According to the schedule, I will now turn to the appellants and ask them, in turn, whether they wish to personally briefly address the -- the Chamber. I will start with Mr. Kubura. Mr. Kubura, do you wish to have a brief personal address to the -- to the Chamber in not more than ten minutes? You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: THE APPELLANT KUBURA: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I did speak a few times in this courtroom. My lawyers submitted in writing all the elements of my appeal, and yesterday they presented their arguments orally as well. In view of everything they said and they wrote, I have nothing to add. I pointed out earlier on, and I'd like to point out now, that I have always trusted this Tribunal, and I repeat that today as well. Thank you for everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Kubura. You may sit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: May I ask Mr. Hadzihasanovic if he wishes to address the Chamber. You have the floor. THE APPELLANT HADZIHASANOVIC: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, I do wish to address you. Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. I do thank you for making it possible for me to address you, and therefore I shall be very brief. The war that broke out in 1991 was a terrible one not only for Bosnia-Herzegovina but for all the republics of the former Yugoslavia. Bosnia and Herzegovina suffered a great deal because of this war, and regrettably it is still suffering to this day. There were many victims in this war, civilians and soldiers, on all sides. I am very sorry for all of them. I am particularly sorry for the victims that pertain to the operations of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and also victims due to actions taken by soldiers that were under my command. I stand before you today as a corps commander who was sentenced by a Trial Chamber because I did not punish, failed to punish soldiers under my command who had committed crimes. Of course, to this day I cannot say that I was a perfect commander in 1993. There are always things that can be done differently, and I keep asking myself all the time whether I could have done more, better. What I can say is that I was a professional soldier who defended his country without any religious, political, or ethnic partiality. I can say that throughout the war I did the best to stop soldiers under my command from committing crimes. Also, I did my best to punish them in accordance with the law if they did commit crimes. Therefore, Your Honours, when I was accused in July 2001 I did not hesitate. I was prepared to appear before this court straight away. I exercised my command in very difficult conditions. As a professional soldier, I could not imagine that such a situation could crop up. I asked my Defence counsel to show to the Court what difficult conditions I had to contend with in the situation, in order to judge the situation as it was then. I think that the Judges did understand up to a degree the situation that I was in then; although, I believe it is very difficult for anyone who was not there to understand what it was like. The presence of Mujahedin in my area was very difficult for me. Al-Qaeda is a well-known concept today, but at that time no one knew who these people were in actual fact and what their real purpose was. I was the first one to have raised that question with my superiors, and I truly believed that they did constitute a great danger. Since I am not a lawyer myself, I hope that you will also try to understand the situation as it was in Central Bosnia in 1993, as well as the measures that I took in order to keep strict discipline within the 3rd Corps that I was in the process of establishing while at the same time fighting. However, although I was sentenced by the Trial Chamber, I still believe in the work of this Tribunal that is good for my Bosnia-Herzegovina. Before I was accused, I testified twice before this Tribunal: In the Blaskic case and in the Krstic case. And before that, I made a statement to Mr. Harmon, the Prosecutor. My trial was a difficult experience for me as an accused person and for my family as well. My life came to a halt when I stood accused. On the other hand, I was always treated well and professionally here and in detention. I was allowed provisional release, which meant a great deal to me, and I wish to express my gratitude to all for that. In conclusion, I can just say that I fully support all the arguments and proposals made by my Defence here, and I do thank you once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Hadzihasanovic. You can sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Well, this concludes the appeals hearing in this case. I wish to thank the parties, counsel for -- also for having kept within the schedule as it was announced, and, of course, all those who assisted in the -- in the hearing in different capacities, with a special mention for the interpreters, whose help is always of primary importance for our discussion. The judgement will be rendered in due course. The Appeal Chamber will now rise.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.40 p.m.
